observable_behaviours: Uses a general search engine (e.g. Google) to find information for an assignment or work task, entering simple keyword queries without applying filters
Navigates to known institutional resources (e.g. library homepage, VLE) when directed, but relies on bookmarks or links provided by others rather than independent navigation
Identifies obviously relevant results from a search results page by reading titles and snippets, without systematically evaluating source type or date
evidence_types: Browser history or search log showing use of general search engines for academic tasks
Submitted assignment containing references sourced from a single search session without database-specific filtering

common_misconceptions.misconception: Using Google Scholar is equivalent to using an academic database
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Google Scholar has limited filtering, inconsistent metadata, and does not provide systematic access to institutional subscriptions in the way that databases like Web of Science or Scopus do

common_misconceptions.misconception: The first page of search results contains the most authoritative sources
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Ranking algorithms optimise for relevance and engagement, not academic authority; highly cited but paywalled or specialist sources often appear lower

context_dependencies.role: Students at this level typically rely on links provided by their tutor via the VLE. Educators may demonstrate basic searching to students but not systematically use advanced filters themselves. Professional services staff tend to search internal intranet or HR portals rather than academic databases.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM students may be directed to specific databases early (PubMed, arXiv) but still use them at a basic level. Humanities students may rely more heavily on library catalogue searches. Differences in search vocabulary across disciplines become a barrier at this level.
context_dependencies.institution_level: HE students are expected to move beyond this level quickly; it is the typical entry point for first-year undergraduates. FE students may remain here longer if information literacy is not explicitly taught.
context_dependencies.region: Minimal regional variation at this level. Institutional library provision affects which resources are practically accessible.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may avoid digital search entirely, preferring physical library visits or asking peers. Moderate-confidence users use search engines fluently but without academic rigour.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): basic search skills are only useful if paired with even minimal evaluation; without 1.2, basic 1.1 produces unreliable results
dc-1-3 (Managing information): at this level, users typically do not manage what they find; a gap between 1.1 and 1.3 is common and expected
assessability: Self-report is unreliable at this level as users often overestimate their search sophistication. Observable evidence (screen recordings, search logs, reference lists in submitted work) is more reliable. Peer tutors and module leaders can assess indirectly through assignment quality.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may use AI chat tools (e.g. ChatGPT) as a substitute for searching, treating AI-generated summaries as primary sources without verification. This is a significant risk behaviour at Basic level that conflates search with AI-assisted retrieval.

observable_behaviours: Uses Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) and quotation marks for phrase searching in library databases and search engines to refine results
Selects appropriate academic databases for a given discipline (e.g. PsycINFO for psychology, JSTOR for humanities) and applies date, language, and document-type filters
Constructs a systematic search strategy for a literature review, documenting search terms, databases used, and number of results retrieved
evidence_types: Annotated bibliography or literature review with documented search methodology and database sources
PRISMA flow diagram or search log spreadsheet showing terms, databases, and inclusion/exclusion decisions

common_misconceptions.misconception: A comprehensive search means searching more databases
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Comprehensiveness depends on selecting the right databases for the research question, not maximising the number searched; irrelevant databases add noise without improving coverage

common_misconceptions.misconception: Once a good set of search terms is established, it can be reused unchanged across databases
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Different databases use different controlled vocabularies (MeSH, Thesaurus of ERIC Descriptors); effective searching requires adapting terms to each database's indexing system

context_dependencies.role: Educators at this level design search tasks for students and can model intermediate search strategies. Researchers use Boolean searching routinely but may not be applying systematic review methodology. Professional services staff (especially library and registry) use structured searches for policy documents and benchmarking data.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Systematic search methodology is a formal requirement in health sciences and social sciences (systematic reviews, meta-analyses). In STEM, preprint servers (arXiv, bioRxiv) require specific search approaches. Humanities researchers may focus on archival and catalogue search strategies not covered by standard database approaches.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Intermediate level is the target for postgraduate students and upper-level undergraduates in research-intensive programmes. Standard for research staff.
context_dependencies.region: UK institutions often teach this through embedded information literacy programmes (often via the library). EU institutions may have varying provision. US institutions tend to address this at point-of-need.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users develop this level naturally through guided practice. High-confidence users may have self-taught Boolean searching but lack awareness of controlled vocabulary.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): intermediate searching produces a richer result set that demands stronger evaluation skills
dc-1-3 (Managing information): systematic search documentation requires reference management tools (Zotero, Mendeley), linking to 1.3 intermediate
assessability: Directly assessable through submitted search methodology sections in dissertations, systematic reviews, or literature reviews. Library staff, supervisors, and research methods tutors can all assess this reliably.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users begin to critically compare AI-generated literature overviews (e.g. Elicit, Consensus) against database search results, recognising that AI tools may miss recent publications, use inconsistent citation metadata, or hallucinate references.

observable_behaviours: Designs and executes a multi-database systematic search strategy with controlled vocabulary, proximity operators, and exploded subject headings, achieving reproducible results
Critically evaluates the coverage, indexing policies, and limitations of different databases to make informed decisions about search design for a specific research question
Trains or advises others (students, research team members) on advanced search methodology, including creation of reusable search strings and search protocol documentation
evidence_types: Published or submitted systematic review with full PROSPERO-registered search protocol
Workshop materials or recorded training session on advanced search strategy design delivered to peers or students

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced searching means finding everything relevant; a thorough search is a complete search
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Even the most rigorous systematic search has coverage limitations; grey literature, conference proceedings, and non-indexed sources require supplementary hand-searching strategies

common_misconceptions.misconception: AI-powered search tools (Semantic Scholar, Elicit) have made Boolean searching obsolete
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: AI semantic search and Boolean search serve different purposes; AI tools are useful for exploratory searching and concept mapping but lack the reproducibility required for systematic reviews

context_dependencies.role: Researchers at this level lead systematic reviews and are involved in methodological decisions about evidence synthesis. Educators design research methods curricula around advanced search. Librarians at this level act as embedded research partners rather than just service providers.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Systematic review methodology is most formalised in health sciences (Cochrane methodology) and education (Campbell Collaboration). In STEM, database-specific API access and citation chaining become important. Humanities researchers at this level work with archival finding aids and specialist catalogues.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Advanced level is appropriate for doctoral students, postdoctoral researchers, and experienced academic staff. Expected as a professional standard for subject librarians.
context_dependencies.region: PROSPERO and Cochrane registration expectations are strongest in UK and EU health research contexts. Open access requirements affect which databases are most productive.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High-confidence users reach this level more readily. Digital anxiety is rarely a barrier at this stage; disciplinary norms and methodological training are the primary gatekeepers.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): advanced search without advanced evaluation produces high-volume but low-quality evidence synthesis
dc-3-4 (Computational thinking): using database APIs and scripted searches links 1.1 advanced to 3.4 intermediate/advanced
assessability: Peer review of systematic review protocols and published search strategies. Direct observation in research team meetings where search design decisions are made. Supervision logs and co-authored methodology sections.
ai_integration_note: Advanced users critically integrate AI-assisted search tools (Elicit, Semantic Scholar, Research Rabbit) alongside traditional databases, explicitly documenting the role of AI in the search process and acknowledging its limitations in reproducibility and citation accuracy.

observable_behaviours: Develops and validates new search methodologies or frameworks for emerging information environments (e.g. social media data, preprint ecosystems, AI-generated content corpora) and publishes or disseminates findings

Leads institution-wide or sector-wide initiatives to improve information retrieval standards, such as co-authoring database coverage guidelines or contributing to systematic review methodology consortia

Critically evaluates and contributes to the scholarly discourse on the changing nature of information search in AI-augmented research environments, including the epistemological implications of AI-mediated retrieval
evidence_types: Published methodology paper on search strategy design or information retrieval in a peer-reviewed journal
Evidence of sector leadership: membership of systematic review methodology panels, invited training at conferences, or contribution to national/international information literacy standards

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced search competence is only relevant to librarians and information scientists
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Evidence synthesis quality across all disciplines depends on advanced search; researchers at this level are methodological leaders regardless of their disciplinary home

common_misconceptions.misconception: Once you have mastered systematic searching, the skills are stable and do not require ongoing development
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: The information landscape is changing rapidly with AI-generated content, preprint proliferation, and retraction crises; highly advanced users continuously update their practice

context_dependencies.role: Typically researchers and senior librarians. Educators at this level embed research-level search methodology into curriculum design and advocate for institutional information literacy strategy.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Highly advanced searching in STEM may involve computational tools (API queries, automated deduplication). In humanities, this level involves expertise in archival systems, finding aids, and non-digitised collections alongside digital search.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Primarily HE and research institutes. Rare in FE except among specialist research-active staff.
context_dependencies.region: Global engagement with information science community. EU open science mandates and UK REF requirements shape the practical expression of this level.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High digital confidence is a baseline here; the differentiator is scholarly contribution to the field, not technical fluency alone.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): inseparable at this level; highly advanced search and evaluation form an integrated evidence literacy practice
dc-3-4 (Computational thinking): automated search pipelines, API queries, and machine learning-assisted screening tools are used at this level
assessability: Publication record, conference presentations, consultancy to systematic review teams, peer recognition. Difficult to assess in routine HE settings; more appropriate for researcher development appraisal or promotion review.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals contribute to emerging methodological guidance on the role of large language models in systematic review screening, citation analysis, and knowledge synthesis, critically examining both the efficiency gains and validity threats of AI-mediated evidence retrieval.

observable_behaviours: Checks whether a source is a recognised institution (university, government body, established news outlet) before including it in academic work
Notices and flags obviously unreliable sources (anonymous authors, lack of date, clearly commercial intent) when directed to do so
Distinguishes between a primary source (original research article) and a secondary source (textbook, news summary) when examples are provided
evidence_types: Reference list in submitted work showing avoidance of obviously unreliable sources (Wikipedia as a primary citation, promotional websites)
Annotated source list where the student has briefly noted why each source was included

common_misconceptions.misconception: A source published by a university must be reliable
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Universities host a wide range of content including student work, opinion pieces, and unreviewed commentary; institutional affiliation does not guarantee peer review or editorial quality

common_misconceptions.misconception: Peer review guarantees that a paper is correct and trustworthy
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Peer review is a quality filter, not a quality guarantee; errors, biased studies, and even fraudulent papers pass peer review; post-publication scrutiny remains essential

context_dependencies.role: Students are the primary group at this level in HE. Educators may identify students operating here and design scaffolded activities. Professional services staff evaluating policy documents operate at a domain-specific version of this level.
context_dependencies.subject_area: In health sciences, students are introduced to evidence hierarchies early; in humanities and arts, the concept of source reliability is more nuanced (opinion and argument are legitimate).
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected entry level for HE students; basic evaluation is typically addressed in first-year academic skills modules.
context_dependencies.region: Media literacy and fake news awareness vary by region; EU Digital Education Action Plan places particular emphasis on this level.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may apply heuristics (fancy website = reliable) rather than evaluating content. Moderate-confidence users can follow a checklist-based approach.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): search quality determines the pool from which evaluation is performed; basic searching limits what is available to evaluate
dc-2-5 (Digital behaviour): critical evaluation of information is foundational to responsible online behaviour
assessability: Reference lists, annotated bibliographies, and in-class exercises. Module tutors and librarians can assess directly. Self-assessment at this level tends to be overconfident.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may not recognise AI-generated text as requiring evaluation. They may treat ChatGPT outputs or AI-summarised content as equivalent to referenced sources, representing a significant new failure mode that did not exist in pre-AI versions of this competency.

observable_behaviours: Applies a structured evaluation framework (e.g. CRAAP test, SIFT method, or lateral reading techniques) to assess currency, relevance, authority, accuracy, and purpose of academic and non-academic sources
Identifies methodological strengths and weaknesses in research articles, including sample size, study design, conflict of interest disclosures, and statistical reporting
Cross-references claims across multiple independent sources before accepting them as reliable, including checking whether cited sources actually support the claims made
evidence_types: Critical literature review section demonstrating explicit evaluation of source quality, not merely description
Research methods seminar contribution or written reflection showing methodological critique of assigned readings

common_misconceptions.misconception: Applying an evaluation checklist (CRAAP test) is sufficient for critical evaluation
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Checklists operationalise evaluation but do not replace disciplinary judgement; a paper can pass all checklist criteria while making claims that are contested within its field

common_misconceptions.misconception: More recent publications are always more reliable than older ones
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Foundational studies may be decades old and still authoritative; recency is one criterion, not the determining one; retracted recent papers are less reliable than older landmark studies

context_dependencies.role: Educators at this level can evaluate sources for curriculum design and model evaluation processes for students. Researchers apply methodological critique to literature reviews. Professional services staff evaluate policy evidence and grey literature.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM relies heavily on quantitative methodological criteria. Social sciences add qualitative research quality frameworks. Humanities apply source criticism and historiographical methods. Health sciences use evidence hierarchies (RCTs, systematic reviews).
context_dependencies.institution_level: Target level for upper-level undergraduates and postgraduates. Core competence for research staff.
context_dependencies.region: Open access publishing and preprint culture (more prevalent post-COVID) mean intermediate evaluators must assess non-peer-reviewed preprints. EU researchers face this more acutely with strong preprint culture.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users apply frameworks consistently. High-confidence users may apply them more flexibly and critically.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): systematic searching skills are required to perform lateral reading effectively
dc-1-3 (Managing information): evaluated sources need to be organised; evaluation notes should be stored with references
assessability: Literature review chapters, critical reading assignments, journal club contributions. Supervisors and research methods tutors are best placed to assess. Portfolio evidence is reliable.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate evaluators begin to assess AI-generated content critically: checking AI-produced summaries against original sources, identifying hallucinated citations, and applying lateral reading to AI-assisted research outputs. They understand that AI fluency is not a proxy for accuracy.

observable_behaviours: Evaluates the epistemological assumptions underlying different research paradigms (positivism, interpretivism, critical theory) and judges how these affect the claims a study can legitimately make

Synthesises contradictory evidence across a body of literature, identifying reasons for divergence (methodological variation, publication bias, disciplinary paradigm differences) rather than defaulting to majority consensus

Designs and delivers training sessions for others on advanced information evaluation, including how to identify predatory journals, evaluate grey literature quality, and assess AI-generated content reliability
evidence_types: Systematic review or meta-analysis quality appraisal section demonstrating use of validated appraisal tools (GRADE, CASP, Newcastle-Ottawa)
Published or peer-reviewed pedagogical resource on information literacy or source evaluation

common_misconceptions.misconception: Expert evaluators do not need structured frameworks because they can judge intuitively
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Even expert evaluators are subject to confirmation bias and disciplinary blind spots; structured frameworks remain valuable as a check, even when applied rapidly

common_misconceptions.misconception: Once a paper is published in a high-impact journal, it does not need further evaluation
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: High-impact journals have published retracted papers, reproducibility failures, and methodologically flawed studies; impact factor is a journal-level metric, not a paper-level quality guarantee

context_dependencies.role: Researchers at this level are recognised within their communities for methodological expertise. Educators embed critical evaluation into discipline-specific research training. Librarians act as evaluation specialists and embedded research partners.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Advanced evaluation in health sciences involves formal quality appraisal tools for systematic reviews. In social sciences, reflexivity and positionality become part of evaluation. In humanities, textual criticism and provenance evaluation are disciplinary forms of advanced information evaluation.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Doctoral and postdoctoral level in HE; expected professional competence for research-active faculty.
context_dependencies.region: EU open science policies and UK Research Integrity Office guidelines create additional evaluation obligations around data availability and registered reports.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a significant variable at this level; advanced evaluation is driven by methodological knowledge, not digital confidence.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): advanced evaluation requires advanced search to access the full evidence base
dc-3-2 (Integrating and re-elaborating digital content): synthesis of evaluated sources is an expression of both 1.2 and 3.2 at advanced level
assessability: Publication quality appraisal sections, PhD thesis literature reviews, research team leadership, peer observation of teaching where evaluation is modelled. Requires domain expertise in the assessor.
ai_integration_note: Advanced evaluators critically assess AI systems themselves as information sources: evaluating training data provenance, model limitations, potential biases, and the epistemological status of AI-generated knowledge claims. They contribute to institutional guidance on AI tool use in research.

observable_behaviours: Contributes to the development of new information evaluation frameworks, quality appraisal tools, or evidence synthesis methodology in response to emerging information challenges (AI-generated content, data fabrication, misinformation ecosystems)
Leads institutional or sector-wide initiatives on information quality, research integrity, or digital media literacy, influencing policy and curriculum
Publishes scholarly work on information evaluation, epistemology, or critical thinking in the context of digital and AI-mediated information environments
evidence_types: Peer-reviewed publications on information literacy, research methodology, or epistemic approaches to AI-generated knowledge
Evidence of policy contribution: national information literacy strategy input, research integrity committee membership, curriculum design leadership at institutional or sector level

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced evaluators are immune to misinformation
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Expertise in evaluation does not eliminate susceptibility to confirmation bias or motivated reasoning, particularly outside one's specialist domain

common_misconceptions.misconception: Information evaluation at this level is only relevant to information scientists and philosophers
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: All researchers, educators, and informed citizens face the challenge of navigating AI-generated misinformation and information overload; highly advanced evaluation skills are increasingly a societal necessity

context_dependencies.role: Senior researchers, professors, information scientists, and policy leads. Rare in professional services except at the level of information governance specialists.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Varies significantly: health sciences engage with evidence synthesis methodology; humanities engage with epistemological and historiographical theory; STEM engages with reproducibility crisis and data integrity.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE and specialist research institutes.
context_dependencies.region: Global community of practice. EU Digital Compass and UNESCO information literacy frameworks represent the policy contexts this level engages with.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: No longer a variable; digital tools are fluently integrated into evaluation practice.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): inseparable at this level
dc-3-1 (Developing digital content): highly advanced evaluators often produce public-facing resources on information literacy and misinformation
assessability: Publication record, invited contributions to methodology consortia, research integrity committee membership. Suitable for academic promotion review, not routine assessment.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the scholarly and policy discourse on what it means to evaluate information in an age of generative AI, LLM hallucination, synthetic media, and AI-curated information feeds. They may advise on or develop AI audit frameworks and epistemic risk assessments for AI tools used in research.

observable_behaviours: Saves found resources in browser bookmarks or a dedicated folder on a personal device, without a consistent naming or organisational system
Uses copy-paste to collect information snippets into a document or note-taking application for later use
Stores references by copying citation details manually into a document, without using reference management software
evidence_types: Submitted work showing manually formatted references, indicating absence of reference management software
Personal folder or bookmark collection showing saved resources, even if disorganised

common_misconceptions.misconception: Saving everything is the same as managing information
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Hoarding digital information without organisation or retrieval strategy creates its own form of information overload; accumulation without curation is not management

common_misconceptions.misconception: Reference management is only needed for long projects like dissertations
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Reference management habits, when established early, prevent duplication, formatting errors, and lost citations; the overhead of starting mid-project is higher than establishing the habit at the outset

context_dependencies.role: First-year students are the primary group at this level. Educators may operate at basic level for personal note-taking while using more sophisticated systems for research. Professional services staff typically manage documents through institutional systems (SharePoint, Teams) with minimal personal curation.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM students may be introduced to reference managers early through lab reports. Humanities students may delay adoption. Social sciences vary by department.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE students. Library induction programmes typically target this level explicitly.
context_dependencies.region: Cloud storage adoption (Google Drive, OneDrive) varies by region and institution; affects how basic information management manifests.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may rely entirely on print or printed copies. Moderate-confidence users use digital folders but without systematic organisation.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): what is found must be stored; basic search produces less to manage
dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): basic information management may inadvertently involve storing personal data without awareness of obligations
assessability: Indirectly assessable through reference list quality in submitted work. Library staff can assess through one-to-one academic skills appointments.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may save AI-generated outputs alongside research sources without distinguishing between them, creating a mixed personal archive where the provenance of information is unclear.

observable_behaviours: Uses reference management software (Zotero, Mendeley, EndNote) to collect, organise, and cite sources, applying folders and tags to structure a project library
Creates and maintains a personal note-taking system (e.g. OneNote, Obsidian, Notion) to organise research notes by theme, project, or source
Applies a consistent file naming and folder structure convention to digital documents across devices and cloud storage platforms
evidence_types: Dissertation or thesis reference list generated from reference management software, showing consistent formatting and complete metadata
Shared project folder or research notebook demonstrating an organised, retrievable filing system

common_misconceptions.misconception: Using a reference manager is only about formatting citations automatically
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Reference managers also support annotation, tagging, PDF organisation, shared libraries, and integration with word processors; using them only for citation output misses most of their value

common_misconceptions.misconception: Cloud storage automatically organises information
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Cloud storage is a filing cabinet, not a knowledge management system; without intentional organisation, cloud storage becomes as difficult to navigate as a local unorganised folder

context_dependencies.role: Postgraduate students and research-active educators are the primary group at this level. Professional services staff managing institutional documents may develop parallel competences using SharePoint or document management systems rather than academic tools.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Research-intensive subjects develop this level earlier. Arts and creative practice disciplines may use different organisational metaphors (portfolios, sketchbooks) that have digital equivalents.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected by the start of postgraduate study in HE. Zotero and Mendeley are commonly taught at this level.
context_dependencies.region: Institutional licensing (Endnote via institutional subscription vs free tools like Zotero) affects tool choice but not competency level.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users adopt these tools readily with guidance. High-confidence users self-discover features and customise their workflows.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): database browser extensions (Zotero connector) link search directly to management
dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): annotation features in reference managers enable recording evaluation notes alongside sources
assessability: Supervisors and dissertation tutors can assess this directly. Reference lists and research portfolios provide evidence. Library skills workshops provide a context for direct observation.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users begin to manage AI tool outputs alongside traditional sources: archiving prompts and AI-generated summaries with source documentation, and using reference managers with custom fields to record AI provenance information (tool, date, prompt).

observable_behaviours: Designs and implements a personal knowledge management (PKM) system that supports synthesis across projects, enabling identification of connections between ideas from different sources and time periods
Manages a shared team or project research library (e.g. shared Zotero group library, institutional repository contribution), including onboarding others and maintaining metadata quality
Creates data management plans that address how research data and associated documentation will be stored, organised, shared, and preserved across the full research lifecycle
evidence_types: Research Data Management Plan submitted to a funder (UKRI, Horizon Europe) or institutional data governance committee
Evidence of contribution to institutional repository (deposit of datasets, publications, or grey literature with complete metadata)

common_misconceptions.misconception: A sophisticated note-taking system is a substitute for deep engagement with sources
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: PKM tools support organisation and retrieval but do not produce synthesis; over-investment in system design at the expense of reading and thinking is a known productivity trap

common_misconceptions.misconception: Data management planning is an administrative compliance exercise, not a research skill
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Effective data management plans save significant time and cost during and after projects; researchers who treat DMP as a compliance box-tick often encounter problems with data reuse, sharing, and reproducibility

context_dependencies.role: Senior researchers and research-active educators. Research data officers and information governance professionals in professional services.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM and health sciences face the strongest funder requirements for data management plans. Social sciences deal with sensitive personal data management. Humanities increasingly engage with digital archiving and long-term preservation.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Advanced level in HE research contexts. Relevant for all research-active staff.
context_dependencies.region: EU Horizon Europe requires DMPs as part of all funded projects. UKRI mandates open data with specific exceptions. UK and EU researchers face more immediate DMP obligations than US counterparts in publicly funded research.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence is typical; the challenge at this level is institutional navigation and funder requirements, not digital skill.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): research data management at advanced level requires GDPR and data protection compliance knowledge
dc-3-4 (Computational thinking): scripted workflows for data organisation and archiving link 1.3 advanced to 3.4
assessability: Funder DMP reviews, institutional research data management audits, peer assessment of shared library quality. Research data management specialists and subject librarians are best placed to assess.
ai_integration_note: Advanced users integrate AI-generated content into formal research data management frameworks: treating AI outputs as a data type requiring provenance documentation, version control, and appropriate retention and disposal policies consistent with institutional data governance.

observable_behaviours: Leads the design and implementation of institutional information management strategies, including research data infrastructure, open access policies, and knowledge asset governance
Develops and publishes frameworks or tools for information management best practice in HE research, adopted by others at institutional or sector level
Advocates for and contributes to national or international standards in research data management, open science infrastructure, or digital preservation
evidence_types: Institutional open access or research data management policy document authored or led
Published framework, tool, or guidance on research information management adopted by other institutions or cited in sector guidance

common_misconceptions.misconception: Information management at the highest level is about personal organisation
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Highly advanced information management is fundamentally about collective and institutional knowledge governance, not just personal efficiency

common_misconceptions.misconception: Open access infrastructure is a technical problem, not an information management one
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Open access requires coordinated information management across discovery, preservation, metadata standards, rights management, and researcher workflows; the technical layer depends on sound information management practice

context_dependencies.role: Chief Information Officers, Research Data Managers at national facilities, senior librarians, and research governance leads. Rare in teaching-only roles.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Cross-disciplinary at this level; national research data infrastructure must serve all disciplines.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE and national research facilities.
context_dependencies.region: EU FAIR data principles, UK UKRN guidelines, UNESCO Open Science Recommendation are the policy contexts at this level.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable; the challenge is institutional leadership and policy influence.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 1 competencies: highly advanced 1.3 is the culmination of an integrated information literacy practice
dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): institutional data governance requires deep integration between information management and data protection
assessability: Institutional leadership record, policy documents, sector-wide contributions, publications. Not assessable in routine HE settings; relevant for professorial or executive appointment review.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape institutional and sector-wide policy on AI-generated content as an information management challenge: provenance standards for AI outputs, AI training data governance, and the long-term preservation implications of AI-dependent research pipelines.

competency_name: Interacting through and with digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Sends and receives email using institutional account, attaching files and responding to messages with basic formatting
Participates in VLE discussion forums by posting responses when required, following prompts from a tutor
Joins scheduled video calls (Teams, Zoom) using a link provided by others, with basic camera and microphone management
evidence_types: Email correspondence with tutor or supervisor demonstrating ability to compose and respond
VLE discussion forum posts submitted as part of assessed module activities

common_misconceptions.misconception: Email is an informal medium equivalent to text messaging
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Institutional email is a professional and sometimes legally significant channel; tone, structure, and record-keeping requirements differ from personal messaging

common_misconceptions.misconception: Being present in a video call is the same as participating effectively
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Passive attendance without contribution does not constitute effective digital interaction; active communication involves structured contribution, turn-taking, and follow-up

context_dependencies.role: Students primarily use institutional email and VLE tools. Educators interact through these plus lecture capture and synchronous teaching platforms. Professional services staff also use Microsoft Teams or Slack as primary communication channels.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation; all HE subjects require basic digital communication through institutional channels.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected from first week of HE enrolment.
context_dependencies.region: Tool choice varies (Teams dominant in UK HE, Zoom more common internationally) but competency description is platform-agnostic.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may avoid asynchronous text communication and over-rely on in-person interaction or phone calls.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-5 (Digital behaviour): tone and conduct in digital communication
dc-2-6 (Managing digital identity): institutional email is part of the managed professional digital identity
assessability: Tutors and administrative staff observe this directly through day-to-day interaction. Measurable through response times, email quality, and VLE engagement data.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may use AI tools to draft emails or forum posts without disclosure; basic interaction competence does not include awareness of the implications of AI-mediated communication.

competency_name: Interacting through and with digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Selects the appropriate digital communication channel (email, Teams chat, video call, VLE announcement) based on urgency, audience, and formality requirements
Facilitates or actively contributes to synchronous online discussions, managing turn-taking and ensuring inclusive participation
Uses collaborative tools (Teams, Slack, shared documents) to coordinate work with peers or colleagues asynchronously across time zones or locations
evidence_types: Evidence of organising and facilitating an online meeting, seminar, or team session
Project documentation showing effective use of collaborative platforms for communication and coordination

common_misconceptions.misconception: Faster communication tools (instant messaging) are always better than slower ones (email)
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Channel appropriateness depends on permanence, searchability, formality, and audience; instant messaging creates fragmented records and notification overload when used for complex or high-stakes communications

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital collaboration is just digital version of face-to-face collaboration
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Asynchronous digital collaboration requires explicit communication of context, structured documentation, and intentional relationship maintenance that differs from co-located working

context_dependencies.role: Educators at this level manage hybrid teaching and blended cohort communications. Researchers coordinate distributed teams and international collaborations. Professional services staff manage cross-departmental communications and student-facing enquiry systems.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation at this level; skills are broadly applicable.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and all academic staff.
context_dependencies.region: International collaborations (common in EU-funded research) place more demands on asynchronous communication competence.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High-confidence users develop this level readily. Moderate-confidence users may default to synchronous (video) over asynchronous channels, creating bottlenecks.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-4 (Collaborating through digital technologies): effective interaction is a prerequisite for effective digital collaboration
dc-2-5 (Digital behaviour): professional norms in digital communication become more important as communication volume and complexity increase
assessability: Observable in team project outcomes, meeting facilitation, and communication artefacts. Module leaders and project supervisors can assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users begin to use AI tools to enhance communication: using AI for translation in multilingual collaborations, AI-generated meeting summaries (Teams Copilot), and AI-drafted communications with explicit editing and review.

competency_name: Interacting through and with digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Designs communication protocols and channel architectures for teams or organisations, balancing information flow, accessibility, and cognitive load
Critically evaluates digital communication tools for their pedagogical, ethical, or organisational implications before adoption or recommendation to others
Advises colleagues or students on effective digital communication practices, including accessibility, inclusion, and professional norms in hybrid environments
evidence_types: Communication protocol or digital collaboration policy document authored for a team, department, or institution
Training or guidance materials on digital communication best practices delivered to peers or students

common_misconceptions.misconception: The best communicators in digital environments are those who communicate most frequently
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Effective digital communication involves signal-to-noise management; high-frequency communicators may generate overload rather than clarity

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced digital communication is about mastering the latest tools
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Advanced competence is about strategic channel design, inclusive communication, and critical evaluation of tools; platform fluency is a lower-level skill

context_dependencies.role: Educators design digital communication environments for students. Research team leaders establish collaboration protocols. Professional services directors manage institutional communication strategy.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Technology and information science disciplines engage most critically with digital communication systems. Education and management disciplines apply this professionally.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Senior academic and professional services roles in HE.
context_dependencies.region: GDPR and data protection requirements affect tool selection (e.g. Microsoft Teams vs Google Workspace vs US-hosted tools) particularly for EU and UK institutions.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence is typical but not the differentiator; critical evaluation of tools distinguishes this level.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): tool selection must account for data protection implications
dc-2-6 (Managing digital identity): strategic communication design connects to how institutional and professional identity is projected digitally
assessability: Leadership roles, policy documents, peer recognition. Observable in how individuals design communication environments, not just how they use them.
ai_integration_note: Advanced users critically evaluate AI communication features (Teams Copilot summaries, AI-generated email drafts, AI-moderated discussions) for their pedagogical appropriateness, accuracy, and implications for authentic student engagement and professional accountability.

competency_name: Interacting through and with digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Shapes institutional or sector-wide norms and policies for digital interaction, including AI-mediated communication, accessibility standards, and hybrid working protocols
Publishes or presents research or thought leadership on the changing nature of human-digital interaction in educational or professional contexts
Contributes to standards bodies or policy forums on digital communication ethics, accessibility, or AI integration in professional communication
evidence_types: Institutional digital communication strategy or policy document with evidence of authorship
Published work or conference keynote on digital interaction in HE or professional contexts

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced digital communication is purely technical expertise
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: At this level the competence is primarily strategic, ethical, and organisational rather than technical

common_misconceptions.misconception: Communication norms established in one cultural or institutional context transfer universally
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Highly advanced practitioners understand that digital communication norms are culturally situated and that global or diverse institutional contexts require deliberate intercultural communication design

context_dependencies.role: Senior institutional leaders, policy advisors, and communication researchers.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Communication studies, education technology, and information science are natural homes; but this level is achievable across disciplines through leadership contribution.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive and policy-leading HE institutions.
context_dependencies.region: EU Digital Decade, UK Online Safety Act, and international accessibility standards shape the policy landscape at this level.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 2 competencies: highly advanced 2.1 integrates across communication, collaboration, identity, and behaviour
assessability: Reputation, publications, institutional leadership roles, policy contributions. Not suitable for routine assessment.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the discourse on AI-mediated communication: what it means for human connection, professional identity, epistemic responsibility, and democratic participation when AI increasingly mediates how we interact in educational and professional contexts.

observable_behaviours: Shares files with classmates or colleagues using email attachments or simple link sharing (Google Drive, OneDrive) when prompted
Posts content (comments, images, documents) in closed institutional spaces (VLE forums, Teams channels) with a basic understanding that the audience is restricted to the course or team
Understands that sharing content publicly is different from sharing within an institutional platform, though may not consistently apply this distinction
evidence_types: Shared document or submission contributed to a group assignment via institutional platform
VLE or Teams post showing participation in a shared space

common_misconceptions.misconception: Anything shared in a university VLE or Teams is private
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Institutional platforms may be accessed by administrators, retained for compliance purposes, or visible to a broader group than expected; institutional does not mean personal and private

common_misconceptions.misconception: Sharing a link to a document is the same as giving someone a copy
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Link sharing creates a live connection to a document that can be revoked or changed; understanding permissions and access control is part of responsible sharing

context_dependencies.role: Students share assignments and resources. Educators share course materials. Professional services share documents and forms.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation; all HE subjects involve basic digital sharing.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE.
context_dependencies.region: Cloud platform availability (Microsoft 365 vs Google Workspace) affects practical expression.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may default to physical document sharing or emailing copies rather than using shared spaces.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): sharing content requires awareness of what can legally be shared
dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): sharing data about others requires appropriate consent and controls
assessability: Observable through group project participation and platform engagement data. Tutors and module leaders can assess indirectly.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may share AI-generated content without attribution or without awareness that sharing AI outputs in academic contexts may have integrity implications.

observable_behaviours: Applies appropriate access controls when sharing digital content (view only, edit, restricted to specific users) based on the sensitivity and purpose of the content
Shares academic work or findings through open channels (open access repositories, ResearchGate, academic social networks) with basic understanding of licensing implications
Attributes sources correctly when sharing or re-posting digital content, including images, data, and others' written work
evidence_types: Open access publication deposit or self-archiving in institutional repository with correct licence selected
Shared project document with appropriate permission settings documented

common_misconceptions.misconception: Making research open access is simply uploading a PDF publicly
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Open access involves choosing appropriate licences (CC BY, CC BY-NC), complying with funder mandates (Green vs Gold), and understanding embargo periods and publisher agreements

common_misconceptions.misconception: If something is publicly available online, it can be freely shared with anyone
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Publicly available content may still be protected by copyright or licensed in ways that restrict redistribution; accessibility does not equal open licence

context_dependencies.role: Researchers share findings through open access channels. Educators share course materials and OERs. Students share group work and engage with academic social platforms.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Health and life sciences face strong funder mandates (UKRI, NIH) for open access. Humanities and arts face more complex copyright situations with primary materials.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate researchers and academic staff.
context_dependencies.region: EU open access mandates (Plan S, Horizon Europe requirements) are more prescriptive than US equivalents. UK UKRI open access policy is mandatory for funded research.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users manage sharing settings independently. High-confidence users extend this to open science workflows.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): sharing and copyright are inseparable
dc-1-3 (Managing information): managing what you intend to share requires good information organisation
assessability: Repository deposits, publication records, open access compliance checks. Supervisors and research development staff can assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate sharers consider the implications of sharing AI-assisted work: attributing AI tool use in shared documents, understanding platform terms of service for AI-generated content, and applying appropriate licences to works with AI-generated components.

observable_behaviours: Designs and implements open sharing strategies for research outputs, datasets, or educational resources, selecting platforms, licences, and metadata standards appropriate to the audience and purpose
Advises colleagues on open access publishing routes, data sharing obligations, and licensing decisions, navigating institutional and funder requirements

Contributes to public scholarship or knowledge exchange through digital channels (institutional blogs, public-facing repositories, policy briefs, preprints) with professional quality and appropriate framing for non-specialist audiences
evidence_types: Deposited open dataset with full metadata and licence documentation meeting FAIR principles
Knowledge exchange output (blog, policy brief, public lecture recording) shared through a professional digital channel

common_misconceptions.misconception: Open access automatically means maximum dissemination and impact
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Open access is a necessary but not sufficient condition for impact; discoverability, metadata quality, and communication strategy are equally important for research to reach intended audiences

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced sharing competence is only relevant for researchers
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Educators sharing OERs, professional services sharing institutional data responsibly, and student advocates sharing campaign materials all require advanced sharing practice in their domains

context_dependencies.role: Researchers lead on open science and data sharing. Educators design OER strategies. Knowledge exchange professionals manage public-facing digital communication.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM and health sciences face the most prescriptive data sharing requirements. Social sciences deal with anonymisation and consent for shared data. Creative disciplines engage with complex licensing of shared creative work.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-active academic and professional services staff.
context_dependencies.region: EU GDPR affects what can be shared about research participants. FAIR data principles are mandated across EU-funded research. UK Concordat on Open Research Data sets expectations.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a significant variable; knowledge of requirements is the differentiator.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): advanced sharing requires expert licence selection
dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): data sharing must comply with data protection obligations
assessability: Open access records, data deposits, knowledge exchange activities. Research development teams and institutional repositories track this.
ai_integration_note: Advanced sharers address the complexities of sharing AI-assisted research: disclosing AI involvement in shared outputs according to journal or repository policies, managing intellectual property questions where AI tools contributed to the work, and contributing to emerging norms around AI attribution in shared academic content.

observable_behaviours: Shapes institutional or sector-wide open access, knowledge exchange, or public engagement strategy, influencing what, how, and with whom knowledge is shared
Contributes to international open science infrastructure or standards (ORCID, DataCite, OpenAIRE, Creative Commons) at a governance or technical level
Publishes or presents on the ethics, governance, and practice of digital knowledge sharing in HE, contributing to scholarly or policy discourse
evidence_types: Institutional open access or research data sharing policy document with evidence of authorship or leadership
Contribution to an international open science organisation, standard, or infrastructure project

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced sharing is just about volume of public outputs
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Strategic, ethically informed, and technically excellent sharing is qualitatively different from high-frequency posting; it includes governance, sustainability, and equity dimensions

common_misconceptions.misconception: Open sharing is inherently democratising and always beneficial
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Open sharing can also expose marginalised researchers to harassment, disclose sensitive data, or create power imbalances between well-resourced and less-resourced institutions; highly advanced practitioners engage with these tensions critically

context_dependencies.role: Research directors, library leaders, knowledge exchange champions, and open science advocates.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Cross-disciplinary leadership.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE and policy-influential institutions.
context_dependencies.region: EU, UK, and international open science policy.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 2 competencies
dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences)
assessability: Leadership contributions, policy documents, sector influence.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape policy on AI and open science: what it means for the integrity of the shared scholarly record when AI can generate plausible but fictitious research, and how attribution, transparency, and reproducibility norms must evolve.

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Participates in online surveys or polls related to university life (student satisfaction surveys, module evaluations) when prompted
Accesses digital public services relevant to student life (student finance portals, NHS registration, council tax exemption) independently
Follows institutional social media accounts or student union digital channels to stay informed about university community matters
evidence_types: Completion of institutional surveys or digital consultations
Use of student services digital portals (demonstrated through registration records or service completion)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Online participation is optional and carries no civic or institutional weight
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Module evaluations, student surveys, and digital consultations directly influence institutional decisions; low response rates reduce the quality of governance and are a form of digital civic disengagement

common_misconceptions.misconception: Engaging in citizenship online means using social media for political commentary
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital citizenship encompasses a much broader range of practices including accessing public services, participating in institutional governance, and engaging with community information

context_dependencies.role: Students engage with student services and institutional governance platforms. Educators engage with professional body digital channels and institutional governance systems. Professional services staff use democratic participation channels within professional communities.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation at basic level.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Relevant from first week of HE enrolment.
context_dependencies.region: Digital public service sophistication varies significantly by region; UK and EU have extensive digital public services; international students face additional navigation challenges.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may avoid digital civic participation, relying on in-person or paper processes where available.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-1 (Interacting through digital technologies): civic participation through digital channels requires basic interaction competence
dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): engaging with digital public services involves sharing personal data
assessability: Participation records in institutional surveys. Direct observation of digital service use is rarely feasible; self-report is the primary method.
ai_integration_note: At this level, AI has minimal direct role; however, AI-curated information feeds may shape what students perceive as the relevant civic or institutional landscape, creating filter bubble effects that limit their awareness of university community matters.

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Uses digital channels to contribute to institutional governance (responding to institutional consultations, participating in staff or student forums that feed into decision-making processes)
Critically evaluates digital civic information, distinguishing between institutional communications, student union campaigns, and third-party advocacy, and responds appropriately to each
Uses digital professional networks (LinkedIn, ResearchGate) to engage with professional communities relevant to their field, contributing constructive and professional content
evidence_types: Submission to an institutional consultation, professional body digital survey, or public consultation on education policy
Professional network profile showing active, constructive engagement with field-relevant community

common_misconceptions.misconception: Professional digital networks are primarily for job hunting
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Professional networks support knowledge sharing, community building, peer learning, and collaborative engagement with professional practice; reducing them to job-seeking misses their civic and professional development functions

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital civic engagement is less meaningful than in-person civic participation
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital participation can reach wider and more diverse communities than in-person engagement; the question is quality of engagement, not medium

context_dependencies.role: Students at this level engage with student union governance and institutional feedback channels. Educators engage with professional body governance and sector policy consultations. Researchers engage with open science and research integrity discourse.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Social sciences, law, and humanities engage with digital civic participation more critically as part of their disciplinary content.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and all academic staff.
context_dependencies.region: EU digital democracy initiatives (DigiComp, Citizens Initiative) create specific engagement opportunities. UK HE governance frameworks (OfS, QAA) involve digital engagement mechanisms.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users engage actively. High-confidence users may disengage through cynicism about digital participation effectiveness.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-5 (Digital behaviour): professional norms are particularly important in civic digital spaces
dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): critically evaluating civic information before responding requires good information evaluation
assessability: Participation records, professional network content, institutional consultation submissions. Self-report is important; peer observation is relevant in professional practice modules.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users begin to notice and critically evaluate AI-generated civic content (deepfakes, AI-produced campaign materials, algorithmically amplified misinformation) in digital civic spaces, developing awareness of how AI shapes digital public discourse.

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Designs or facilitates digital civic engagement initiatives within or beyond the institution (online consultations, digital student forums, civic tech projects) with attention to inclusivity and accessibility
Advocates for responsible and equitable digital civic participation, identifying barriers (connectivity, literacy, language) and addressing them in practice
Engages critically with digital political and policy processes relevant to HE (Open University legislation, education funding policy, AI regulation) through public channels
evidence_types: Design documentation or evaluation report for a digital civic engagement initiative
Published commentary, policy response, or public advocacy on HE-relevant digital policy

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced digital civic engagement means building civic technology platforms
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Building platforms is one expression of advanced competence; equally important is advocacy, facilitation, and critical engagement with existing civic digital systems

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital civic engagement is politically neutral
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital platforms embed design choices that advantage certain voices and viewpoints; advanced practitioners recognise and challenge these biases

context_dependencies.role: Student engagement professionals, civic-minded academic staff, public policy researchers.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Politics, public administration, education, communication studies, and law are natural disciplinary homes.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Mid-career and senior HE staff and advanced researchers.
context_dependencies.region: EU democratic participation frameworks and UK post-Brexit civic landscape create different engagement contexts.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence; the challenge at this level is strategic and political, not technical.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies): public advocacy involves strategic digital sharing
dc-3-1 (Developing digital content): creating effective civic communication content
assessability: Project leadership, published advocacy, institutional contributions. Relevant for promotion and leadership review.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners engage critically with the implications of AI for digital democracy: algorithmic content curation, AI-generated political content, AI in electoral systems, and the responsibility of HE to develop AI-literate citizens capable of participating effectively in AI-mediated civic spaces.

competency_name: Engaging in citizenship through digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Leads institutional, national, or international initiatives at the intersection of digital technology and civic participation, influencing policy, practice, and public discourse
Publishes or presents on digital citizenship, digital democracy, or the civic implications of AI in educational or policy contexts
Contributes to governance bodies or advisory panels on digital civic participation, AI regulation, or technology policy at national or international level
evidence_types: Policy advisory role, committee membership, or published submission on digital civic participation or technology regulation
Peer-reviewed or widely cited publication on digital citizenship in HE or society

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced digital civic engagement is only for politicians and policy professionals
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Academics, educators, and researchers have a distinct civic role in informing public discourse and shaping technology policy; their expertise is valuable in civic spaces

common_misconceptions.misconception: Influencing digital policy requires technical expertise in AI or platform design
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Policy influence at this level requires ethical reasoning, pedagogical insight, and social analysis; technical expertise is useful but not prerequisite

context_dependencies.role: Senior academics, policy researchers, civic tech leaders.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Politics, sociology, education, law, and information science.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive and policy-influential institutions.
context_dependencies.region: EU and UK regulatory landscapes; global digital rights discourse.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 2 competencies
dc-4-3 (Supporting wellbeing): digital citizenship includes attention to civic wellbeing in digital environments
assessability: Policy contributions, publications, leadership roles.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape national and international policy on AI and democratic participation, contributing to frameworks for AI transparency, accountability, and the protection of digital democratic rights.

observable_behaviours: Contributes to a shared document (Google Docs, Word Online) when added to an existing collaboration by a peer or tutor
Participates in a group chat or channel on Teams or WhatsApp for a project, reading and posting messages as required
Completes an assigned section of a group task using shared digital tools, with minimal coordination beyond what is explicitly scheduled
evidence_types: Edit history in a shared group document showing contribution
Group project submission demonstrating participation across team members' sections

common_misconceptions.misconception: Online collaboration is simply dividing a task and working separately
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Effective digital collaboration involves iterative co-creation, feedback loops, version management, and integration of contributions; sequential division is co-production without collaboration

common_misconceptions.misconception: The person who organises the shared folder has done the collaboration work
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Administrative setup is not collaboration; the substantive collaborative work involves contributing ideas, responding to others, and integrating feedback

context_dependencies.role: Students collaborate on group assignments. Educators collaborate with colleagues on course materials. Professional services staff collaborate on reports and projects.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Group work is more common in some disciplines than others; professional programmes (business, health, education) embed team working more explicitly.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected from first year of HE; increasingly scaffolded in module design.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may resist digital collaboration, preferring to meet in person and produce a physical document.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-1 (Interacting through digital technologies): communication is a prerequisite for collaboration
dc-1-3 (Managing information): shared document management is a prerequisite for effective digital collaboration
assessability: Group project outcomes, peer assessment, document edit histories. Tutors observe through group presentation and product quality.
ai_integration_note: At this level, AI collaboration tools (Copilot in Word, AI editors in Google Docs) may be available but are used passively, with limited awareness of their implications for group contribution attribution.

observable_behaviours: Coordinates a digital collaborative project, establishing shared norms (response time expectations, version control conventions, task allocation) and maintaining momentum across asynchronous team members
Uses project management tools (Trello, Asana, MS Planner) to track collaborative tasks, deadlines, and responsibilities in a team context
Provides and receives constructive feedback through collaborative platforms, using annotation tools, commenting features, and revision tracking
evidence_types: Shared project management board or task tracker showing coordinated team workflow
Annotated collaborative document showing constructive feedback exchange and revision history

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital collaboration tools solve coordination problems automatically
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Tools provide infrastructure; coordination requires explicit communication of expectations, regular check-ins, and conflict management; no tool substitutes for this relational work

common_misconceptions.misconception: Real-time collaboration (everyone editing simultaneously) is always better than asynchronous collaboration
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Real-time collaboration suits certain tasks (brainstorming, joint drafting) but creates coordination overhead and timezone barriers for distributed teams; asynchronous workflows are often more effective for sustained production

context_dependencies.role: Educators coordinate curriculum development teams. Researchers manage distributed research projects. Students lead peer-assessed group work. Professional services staff manage cross-departmental projects.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM research collaborations often use specialised tools (GitHub, Jupyter notebooks, OSF). Humanities collaborations may focus on shared annotation and archival tools.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Postgraduate students and professional staff.
context_dependencies.region: International research collaborations require asynchronous-first collaboration strategies due to time zone differences.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users coordinate effectively with guidance. High-confidence users adapt tools to team needs.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-1 (Interacting through digital technologies): effective interaction underpins coordination
dc-3-4 (Computational thinking): research collaborations increasingly involve coordinated data pipelines and shared code repositories
assessability: Project documentation, peer assessment, team reflection logs. Module leaders and supervisors observe through project outcomes.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate collaborators begin to integrate AI tools into collaborative workflows: AI writing assistance in shared documents, AI meeting summarisation, and awareness of the need to establish team norms around AI tool use, attribution, and quality checking.

observable_behaviours: Designs digital collaboration environments for research teams or educational cohorts, selecting and configuring tools to support specific collaboration goals (co-authorship, data sharing, peer review, co-design)
Leads interdisciplinary or international digital collaborations, managing cultural, disciplinary, and technical differences in collaborative practice
Critically evaluates digital collaboration tools for their fit with team needs, accessibility, data security, and ethical implications before implementation
evidence_types: Research collaboration protocol or team working agreement document for an active project
Evidence of leading an interdisciplinary or international collaborative project to successful completion

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced collaboration competence means using the most sophisticated tools available
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Advanced competence is about matching tools to team needs and designing effective collaboration environments; over-engineering with complex tools can impede rather than support collaboration

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital collaboration removes the need for relationship building
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Effective digital collaboration, especially long-term or high-stakes, requires deliberate relationship investment; trust cannot be outsourced to collaboration platforms

context_dependencies.role: Research Principal Investigators, curriculum design leads, cross-functional professional services project managers.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Varies by disciplinary collaboration norms and typical project scales.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Mid-career and senior HE staff.
context_dependencies.region: EU Horizon Europe requires cross-national collaboration; UK UKRI prioritises interdisciplinary partnership.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence is typical.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies): collaboration outputs need to be shared appropriately
dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): collaboration across institutions raises data governance questions
