assessability: Research outputs, project reports, team evaluations, grant reports. Peer review and stakeholder feedback.
ai_integration_note: Advanced collaborators design AI-integrated collaboration environments: establishing team norms for AI-assisted co-authorship, managing attribution when AI tools contribute to shared work, and evaluating how AI writing and coding assistants affect quality, voice, and equity within collaborative teams.

observable_behaviours: Shapes institutional or sector-wide digital collaboration infrastructure, policy, and culture through strategic leadership and advocacy
Contributes to international research collaboration standards, open science platforms, or collaborative technology governance
Publishes or presents on the future of digital collaboration in HE, including the implications of AI for collaborative knowledge production
evidence_types: Institutional digital collaboration strategy or research infrastructure initiative led
International collaboration platform governance contribution or published research on digital collaboration

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced collaboration means collaborating with the most people
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Network size is not a quality indicator; deep, productive, ethically managed collaborations that advance knowledge are the hallmark of highly advanced practice

common_misconceptions.misconception: AI collaboration tools will eventually make human coordination redundant
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Human collaboration involves trust, negotiation, creative friction, and shared meaning-making that current AI cannot replicate; highly advanced collaborators understand and articulate the irreducible value of human collaborative processes

context_dependencies.role: Research VPs, collaboration platform developers, open science leads.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Cross-disciplinary.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE.
context_dependencies.region: Global research infrastructure and open science policy.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 2 competencies
assessability: Leadership record, policy contributions, publications.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals contribute to shaping norms for human-AI collaborative knowledge production in research, addressing questions of authorship, intellectual contribution, reproducibility, and the future of peer review in an AI-augmented scholarly ecosystem.

observable_behaviours: Communicates professionally in institutional digital channels (emails to tutors and administrative staff), adapting tone for institutional contexts as distinct from personal social media
Avoids obviously harmful or inappropriate content (offensive language, sharing others' personal information) in institutional digital spaces
Recognises when online communication has become inappropriate and disengages or seeks help from a trusted person
evidence_types: Email communication with institutional staff demonstrating appropriate tone and register
Absence of conduct complaints from institutional digital spaces

common_misconceptions.misconception: Online behaviour has fewer consequences than in-person behaviour
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital communications are often more persistent, more widely shareable, and more legally consequential than in-person interactions; the informal feel of digital spaces does not reduce accountability

common_misconceptions.misconception: Institutional digital platforms are personal spaces
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: VLE forums, institutional email, and Teams channels are professional environments with institutional policies; content posted there may be reviewed by administrators or used in disciplinary processes

context_dependencies.role: All HE users. Students are the primary group at this level, where digital conduct policies first become practically relevant.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation; digital behaviour norms are institutional rather than disciplinary.
context_dependencies.institution_level: From first week of HE.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation in core norms; some variation in legal context (defamation law, harassment law differ across jurisdictions).
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may have less digital behaviour awareness due to less prior exposure to institutional digital contexts.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-6 (Managing digital identity): behaviour in digital spaces shapes the digital identity that others perceive
dc-4-3 (Supporting wellbeing): negative digital behaviour impacts both perpetrators and recipients
assessability: Primarily observable through conduct incidents; proactive assessment through reflection exercises or digital citizenship workshops. Student services and personal tutors may have relevant observations.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may not recognise that using AI to generate aggressive, harassing, or deceptive communications (AI-written phishing, AI-generated fake feedback) is a form of harmful digital behaviour and may have disciplinary and legal consequences.

observable_behaviours: Applies the institution's digital conduct policies, academic integrity policies, and social media guidance in their own practice and can explain the reasoning behind them to peers
Responds constructively to online conflict or inappropriate digital behaviour, using de-escalation strategies or reporting mechanisms rather than retaliation
Models inclusive digital behaviour in collaborative spaces, actively considering the accessibility, tone, and impact of their digital communications on diverse audiences
evidence_types: Peer observation or reflection showing appropriate handling of a digital conduct challenge
Evidence of contributing to digital community norms (e.g. helping establish ground rules for an online group or forum)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Reporting inappropriate digital behaviour is unhelpful or escalatory
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Reporting is the mechanism through which institutions address systematic digital misconduct; failure to report allows harmful behaviour to continue and normalise

common_misconceptions.misconception: AI-assisted communication is always more professional because it sounds more formal
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: AI-generated text may mask authentic voice, conceal intent, or produce formally correct but contextually inappropriate communication; professionalism is about contextual appropriateness, not surface formality

context_dependencies.role: Educators model and teach digital behaviour norms. Researchers navigate professional digital spaces with career implications. Professional services staff manage institutional digital environments.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Education, communication, and social science disciplines engage with digital behaviour as academic content as well as practice.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for all staff and postgraduate students.
context_dependencies.region: Online harassment law and defamation frameworks vary by jurisdiction; UK Online Safety Act creates specific obligations.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users engage appropriately. High-confidence users may be overexposed to online conflict and develop defensive or dismissive responses.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-3 (Engaging in citizenship): constructive digital civic engagement depends on sound digital behaviour
dc-2-4 (Collaborating): effective digital collaboration depends on trusted, respectful digital behaviour
assessability: Peer and supervisor observation, reflection portfolios, incident records. Personal tutors and student services staff are often best placed.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users understand and apply institutional policies on AI use: understanding that using AI to impersonate others, generate misleading content, or commit academic dishonesty is a digital behaviour violation with institutional consequences.

observable_behaviours: Designs and delivers digital behaviour training or educational resources for students or staff, including academic integrity, online harassment prevention, and responsible AI use
Contributes to the development or review of institutional digital conduct policies, codes of practice for online teaching, or AI use guidelines
Advocates for positive digital culture change within a team, department, or institution, addressing systemic barriers to inclusive and responsible digital practice
evidence_types: Digital behaviour or academic integrity training materials developed and delivered
Contribution to institutional policy on digital conduct, social media, or AI use

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital behaviour training is only for students
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Staff digital behaviour norms, particularly around AI use, social media, and student communication, require the same deliberate development; some of the most consequential digital behaviour issues in HE involve staff

common_misconceptions.misconception: Positive digital culture emerges naturally in good teams
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Without deliberate attention to norms, expectations, and inclusion, even high-performing teams replicate dominant culture defaults; positive digital culture requires active cultivation

context_dependencies.role: Student experience professionals, academic staff with pastoral or leadership roles, HR and organisational development staff.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Education, communication, and applied ethics disciplines engage with digital behaviour professionally.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Mid-career and senior HE staff.
context_dependencies.region: UK Online Safety Act and EU AI Act create specific regulatory contexts for advanced digital behaviour competence.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a significant variable at this level.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-3 (Digital citizenship): digital behaviour and civic engagement are deeply connected
dc-4-3 (Supporting wellbeing): designing positive digital culture requires attention to wellbeing
assessability: Policy contributions, training delivery records, institutional peer recognition.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners design institutional frameworks for responsible AI use that address digital behaviour: disclosure norms, impersonation risks, AI-generated misinformation, and the blurring of authentic and AI-mediated voice in professional and academic communication.

observable_behaviours: Shapes national or international discourse on digital behaviour, online harassment, AI-mediated communication, and digital ethics through publications, policy work, or advocacy
Leads the development of sector-wide standards, frameworks, or regulatory guidance on digital conduct in HE or professional contexts
Contributes to interdisciplinary research on digital behaviour, online harm, or AI ethics published in peer-reviewed venues or influencing policy
evidence_types: Published research, policy contribution, or sector guidance on digital behaviour, online harm, or AI ethics
Leadership of a national or international initiative on digital conduct in education or professional contexts

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced digital behaviour expertise is purely regulatory or legal
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: It encompasses pedagogy, organisational psychology, ethics, and technology design; legal compliance is a floor, not a ceiling

common_misconceptions.misconception: Technology companies are better placed than educators to shape digital behaviour norms
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Educators bring pedagogical expertise, understanding of developmental context, and attention to equity that technology companies lack; the HE sector has a critical role in shaping digital behaviour norms

context_dependencies.role: Senior researchers, policy advisors, sector leaders.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Education, law, communication, psychology, and information science.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive and policy-influential institutions.
context_dependencies.region: Global digital governance and AI ethics discourse.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 2 competencies
dc-4-3 (Supporting wellbeing)
assessability: Publications, policy contributions, sector leadership.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the scholarly and regulatory frameworks for AI and digital behaviour: what obligations AI developers, platforms, and institutions have to prevent AI-enabled harm, and how digital behaviour norms must evolve in response to generative AI capabilities.

observable_behaviours: Creates and maintains a basic institutional profile (student record, staff directory entry) with accurate and appropriate information
Understands that different digital contexts require different identity presentations (institutional email vs personal social media vs public profiles) and makes basic distinctions in practice
Keeps personal passwords and login credentials secure, not sharing institutional credentials with others
evidence_types: Institutional profile (student record, staff page) showing accurate, appropriate self-representation
Basic password hygiene demonstrated through security training completion record

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital identity is fixed and the same in all contexts
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Effective digital identity management involves contextually appropriate self-presentation; what is appropriate on LinkedIn differs from a VLE profile, which differs from a public Twitter account

common_misconceptions.misconception: Managing digital identity only matters if you have something to hide
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Active digital identity management is a professional competence; not managing your digital presence means others (including AI-powered search tools) construct your digital identity for you

context_dependencies.role: Students manage identity across student life and transition to employability platforms. Educators manage institutional profiles and public professional identity. Professional services staff manage institutional-facing profiles.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation at basic level.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation in core identity management; GDPR affects what institutions can collect and display.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may avoid creating digital profiles, resulting in an absence of managed digital identity.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): personal data shared in identity profiles requires protection
dc-2-5 (Digital behaviour): how one behaves online is inseparable from the identity one projects
assessability: Institutional profile completeness. Career services and personal tutors can assess through guidance sessions.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may not be aware that AI systems aggregate and process their digital footprints to construct representations of them; basic digital identity management does not address this level of identity exposure.

observable_behaviours: Constructs and maintains a professional digital identity across relevant platforms (ORCID, LinkedIn, institutional profile, ResearchGate) with consistent and purposeful self-presentation
Manages privacy settings across digital platforms to control what is visible to different audiences (colleagues, employers, public, institutional systems)
Monitors their digital footprint by periodically searching for their own name and reviewing what information is publicly associated with them
evidence_types: ORCID or LinkedIn profile showing consistent, professionally managed self-presentation
Documentation of a privacy audit across personal and professional digital platforms

common_misconceptions.misconception: Privacy settings on social platforms fully protect your digital identity
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Platform privacy settings are one layer of control; third-party data brokers, screenshots, cached content, and algorithmic profiling operate outside platform settings

common_misconceptions.misconception: Creating an ORCID or LinkedIn profile completes digital identity management
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Creating profiles is a starting point; regular updating, curation of outputs, and active engagement with professional community are the ongoing practice of identity management

context_dependencies.role: Researchers use ORCID and academic networks for research identity. Educators build professional reputation through teaching profiles and social media. Students manage transition from student to professional digital identity. Professional services staff develop sector-specific professional identities.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Researchers in all disciplines benefit from strong research identity management for citation, grant applications, and collaboration discovery.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and all staff.
context_dependencies.region: GDPR (EU/UK) gives individuals more rights to control digital identity data than in many other regions.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users manage this actively. High-confidence users are prolific online but may lack strategic curation of their digital identity.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): identity management and data protection are deeply linked
dc-2-3 (Engaging in citizenship): professional digital identity influences how one's civic engagement is received
assessability: Career services advisors, supervisors, and professional development programmes assess this through portfolio review and coaching sessions.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users begin to understand that AI systems (recommendation engines, hiring algorithms, research profiling tools) construct automated representations of them from their digital footprint; they take initial steps to manage their AI-generated profile by curating outputs and managing platform data.

observable_behaviours: Designs and manages a strategic digital presence that actively supports their professional goals (research impact, teaching reputation, public engagement) with deliberate platform selection and content curation
Advises students or junior colleagues on professional digital identity development, including platforms, self-presentation strategies, and privacy management in academic and professional contexts

Navigates complex digital identity situations: managing institutional vs personal identity boundaries, responding to reputational threats online, or representing an institution in public digital spaces
evidence_types: Evidence of a strategically managed digital presence across multiple professional platforms with clear professional narrative
Career or professional development guidance provided to students or peers on digital identity management

common_misconceptions.misconception: A large online following is evidence of effective digital identity management
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Reach and influence depend on audience alignment and content quality; a focused, professional presence in the right networks is more strategically effective than broad visibility in the wrong ones

common_misconceptions.misconception: Once a professional digital identity is established, it manages itself
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital identity requires ongoing curation; academic profiles, publication records, and professional affiliations change over time and require regular updating to remain accurate and strategically effective

context_dependencies.role: Research-active academics manage complex identity portfolios (researcher, educator, public intellectual, institutional representative). Senior professional services staff manage institutional identity alongside personal professional identity.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Researchers with public engagement obligations manage identity across specialist and public audiences simultaneously.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Mid-career and senior HE staff.
context_dependencies.region: In some regional contexts, public digital visibility carries political risks for academics that must be carefully managed.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence is typical; the challenge is strategic and contextual.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-5 (Digital behaviour): advanced identity management requires exemplary digital behaviour
dc-3-1 (Developing digital content): creating quality content is central to managing professional digital identity
assessability: Portfolio review, peer observation, career development discussions.
ai_integration_note: Advanced users critically engage with how AI tools construct, represent, and rank them: monitoring how they appear in AI-powered search and recommendation systems, understanding the algorithmic logic of research discovery platforms, and managing AI-generated summaries of their work for accuracy.

observable_behaviours: Contributes to institutional, sector, or policy frameworks for managing digital identity in HE, addressing AI profiling, data rights, and professional digital identity standards
Publishes or presents on digital identity, algorithmic profiling, or data rights in educational or professional contexts
Leads institutional initiatives on digital identity governance, including researcher identity systems, institutional profile management, and AI-generated identity representation
evidence_types: Published work or policy contribution on digital identity in HE or professional contexts
Institutional digital identity governance initiative led

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital identity governance is primarily a technical concern
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital identity governance involves legal rights, ethical obligations, pedagogical implications, and power dynamics; the technical layer serves these higher-order concerns

common_misconceptions.misconception: Individuals have full control over their digital identity if they use privacy settings correctly
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: The ecosystem of data brokers, AI profiling systems, and platform algorithmic representations means that individual privacy settings address only a fraction of digital identity construction; systemic change requires policy and governance intervention

context_dependencies.role: Senior researchers, information governance leads, technology ethicists, HR leaders.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Law, information science, communication, and education.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive and governance-leading institutions.
context_dependencies.region: EU GDPR, UK Data Protection Act, and emerging AI Act provisions directly relevant.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): at this level, identity governance and data protection are inseparable
All Area 2 competencies
assessability: Publications, policy contributions, institutional governance roles.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the discourse on AI-mediated identity: what rights individuals and institutions have when AI systems construct representations of them, and what governance frameworks are needed to ensure accuracy, fairness, and contestability of AI-generated digital identities.

observable_behaviours: Creates basic digital documents (Word, PowerPoint, Google Docs) for academic assignments using templates and built-in formatting tools
Produces simple digital media (photographs taken on a smartphone, short videos recorded for a module task) and uploads them to institutional platforms
Edits text-based digital content (blog posts, forum contributions, email) with attention to basic grammar and appropriate register for the institutional context
evidence_types: Submitted digital assignment (essay, presentation, report) demonstrating basic formatting and production
Module task involving digital media creation (recorded presentation, photograph-based submission)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Using a template means you have not really created the content
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Templates scaffold the production process; the quality of content, argument, and communication is independent of whether a template was used

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital content creation is primarily about technical tools, not communication
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: The purpose of digital content creation is always communication; tool proficiency without clear communication goals produces technically competent but purposeless content

context_dependencies.role: Students create course assignments. Educators create course materials and lecture slides. Professional services staff produce reports and communications.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation; all disciplines require basic digital content creation for academic work.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE.
context_dependencies.region: Platform availability (Microsoft 365 vs Google Workspace) varies by institution.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may rely heavily on templates and avoid formatting; moderate-confidence users customise templates and add media.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): creating content that includes others' material requires copyright awareness
dc-3-2 (Integrating and re-elaborating): basic creation is a prerequisite for integration and re-elaboration
assessability: Submitted assignments directly demonstrate this competency. Module tutors assess as part of standard assignment marking.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may use AI writing tools (ChatGPT, Copilot) to generate text content for assignments without evaluating or editing the output, treating AI-generated text as their own created content without understanding the implications for learning and integrity.

observable_behaviours: Creates purposeful digital content for specific audiences, selecting appropriate formats (infographic, video, interactive presentation, data visualisation, podcast) based on communication goals
Applies principles of accessible content design (alt text, captions, colour contrast, readable fonts) to digital content produced for institutional or public sharing
Uses digital production tools beyond basic office software (video editing software, image editing, web authoring tools, screencast recording) to create polished educational or professional content
evidence_types: Digital portfolio, e-learning resource, or multimedia assignment demonstrating purposeful format selection and accessible design
Digital content created for a real audience (department newsletter, student-facing guide, public engagement resource)

common_misconceptions.misconception: More multimedia means better content
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Format choices should serve communication goals; adding video or animation to content that could be more effectively communicated in text adds production overhead without improving learning or communication

common_misconceptions.misconception: Accessibility is a specialist concern only relevant when you know you have disabled audience members
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Accessible design benefits all users, including those on mobile devices, in poor lighting conditions, and with different learning preferences; designing for accessibility is designing for quality

context_dependencies.role: Educators create learning resources, lecture materials, and educational media. Researchers create dissemination materials and public engagement content. Students create coursework in multiple formats and employability portfolios.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Creative arts students engage with digital content creation as disciplinary practice. Education students create teaching resources. STEM students produce data visualisations and technical documentation.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and teaching staff.
context_dependencies.region: WCAG accessibility standards are particularly mandated in UK and EU public sector contexts; the Public Sector Bodies Accessibility Regulations apply to HE in UK.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users produce accessible, purposeful content with guidance. High-confidence users experiment with new formats independently.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): using images, audio, and video requires licence awareness
dc-3-2 (Integrating and re-elaborating): intermediate content creation involves adapting and combining existing material
assessability: Portfolio assessment, e-learning resource review, accessibility audit of produced content. Learning technologists and module tutors assess directly.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate content creators use AI tools (Canva AI, DALL-E for images, AI voiceover tools) to support content production, while beginning to evaluate the appropriateness, accuracy, and bias of AI-generated media components and considering disclosure to audiences.

observable_behaviours: Designs and produces complex digital learning environments, digital publications, or interactive media that demonstrate sophisticated understanding of audience, pedagogy, and production quality
Leads digital content development projects for institutional or public contexts, coordinating across designers, technologists, and subject experts to produce high-quality outputs
Critically evaluates the pedagogical, ethical, and accessibility dimensions of digital content production, advising others and contributing to institutional standards
evidence_types: Institutional e-learning course, open educational resource, or digital publication produced for a real audience with evidence of quality assurance and accessibility
Leadership role in a digital content or media production project with documented outcomes and impact

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced content creators must be expert in every production tool
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Advanced competence involves knowing when to use which tools and how to direct or collaborate with specialists; breadth of tool knowledge is less important than strategic command of production processes

common_misconceptions.misconception: Professional production quality requires expensive tools and software
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Quality is determined by instructional design, communication clarity, and accessibility; sophisticated content can be produced with freely available tools when the creator understands production principles

context_dependencies.role: Learning designers, academic staff with e-learning responsibilities, research communication specialists, public engagement leads.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Education and communication disciplines engage with content creation as professional practice. All disciplines produce content for research dissemination and public engagement.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Senior academic and professional services staff in HE.
context_dependencies.region: OER (Open Educational Resources) movement and Creative Commons licensing shape the advanced content creation landscape globally.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence; the differentiator at this level is pedagogical and strategic thinking.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies): advanced content is created for sharing; sharing strategy is integral to production
dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): expert licence management is required for complex content involving multiple source materials
assessability: Portfolio of produced works, project documentation, peer review of educational resources. Learning technologists and educational development specialists assess.
ai_integration_note: Advanced content creators develop institutional frameworks for AI-assisted content production: defining quality standards, disclosure requirements, and pedagogical integrity norms for content that incorporates AI-generated text, images, voiceover, or interactive elements.

observable_behaviours: Shapes the field of digital content and media production in HE through publications, leadership of national/international OER initiatives, or contribution to production standards and frameworks
Contributes to scholarly understanding of how digital content design affects learning, engagement, and equity in HE contexts
Leads transformative institutional digital content strategies, embedding accessible, open, and pedagogically excellent content production as a core institutional capability
evidence_types: Published research or sector-leading resource on digital content design in HE
Leadership of a national OER initiative, open textbook project, or digital content strategy with measurable institutional or sector impact

common_misconceptions.misconception: The highest level of digital content creation is about producing the most technically sophisticated content
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: At this level, the contribution is conceptual, strategic, and scholarly: shaping norms, evidence, and infrastructure for digital content creation in HE; technical sophistication is a means, not an end

common_misconceptions.misconception: Open educational resources are a lower-quality alternative to proprietary content
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: OERs produced at this level reflect the highest standards of accessibility, pedagogy, and technical quality; open licence is a distribution choice, not a quality indicator

context_dependencies.role: Educational technologists with scholarly profiles, academic staff with digital pedagogy expertise, national OER leads.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Education, information science, communication; cross-disciplinary leadership.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE.
context_dependencies.region: UNESCO OER Recommendation, EU Digital Education Action Plan, and national OER initiatives are the policy contexts.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 3 competencies
dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies)
assessability: Publication record, OER leadership, institutional strategy contributions.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals contribute to the scholarly and policy discourse on AI-generated content in education: what it means for learning design, student development, pedagogical integrity, and the future of human creativity in an age of generative AI.

observable_behaviours: Combines images, text, and simple graphics into a basic digital document (adding a chart to a report, inserting an image into a presentation) using standard office tools
Edits existing digital templates by replacing placeholder content with relevant text and images without altering the underlying structure
Copies and pastes content from multiple digital sources into a single document, with basic awareness that attribution is required
evidence_types: Assignment incorporating multiple content types (text, images, tables) in a single document
Edited or personalised template showing ability to substitute content within an existing structure

common_misconceptions.misconception: Combining content from multiple sources is the same as synthesising it
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Collation (putting things together) is distinct from synthesis (integrating into a coherent new argument or narrative); basic integration stops at collation

common_misconceptions.misconception: If you change the words, you have created original content
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Paraphrasing without attribution and without added intellectual contribution is still a form of uncredited re-use; re-elaboration requires transformative intellectual work, not just textual reformulation

context_dependencies.role: All HE users at entry level.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation at basic level.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users stick to text-only documents; moderate-confidence users add images and basic graphics.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): integrating others' content requires copyright awareness
dc-3-1 (Developing digital content): basic content development is a prerequisite for integration
assessability: Assignment quality and citation practice. Tutors and academic skills staff assess through work product review.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may integrate AI-generated text or images into their work without adequate critical review, treating AI output as equivalent to independently produced content and failing to attribute or evaluate it.

observable_behaviours: Synthesises and re-presents information from multiple digital sources into a coherent, purposeful piece of work, adding original analysis or contextualisation (annotated bibliography, literature review, synthesis report)
Adapts existing digital content (a dataset, a published resource, an OER) for a new audience or purpose, with appropriate attribution and licence compliance
Embeds and links digital objects (datasets, interactive visualisations, external resources) within a document or web-based resource to create an enriched, integrated knowledge product
evidence_types: Literature review or synthesis report demonstrating integration of multiple sources into an original analytical framework
Adapted educational resource based on an existing OER with documented adaptation and attribution

common_misconceptions.misconception: A longer literature review with more sources is always a better synthesis
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Synthesis quality depends on analytical coherence and original interpretation, not volume; a concise, insightful synthesis of fewer sources is more valuable than a lengthy description of many

common_misconceptions.misconception: Adapting someone else's content for your own use is automatically a breach of copyright
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Many resources are published under Creative Commons or similar licences that permit adaptation under specified conditions; understanding what adaptation rights are granted by a licence is an intermediate competence

context_dependencies.role: Students synthesise for dissertations and coursework. Educators adapt OERs and produce adapted teaching resources. Researchers synthesise literature and produce review articles.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Humanities focuses on textual synthesis and interpretation. STEM combines data, visualisations, and literature. Social sciences integrate qualitative and quantitative sources.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and all academic staff.
context_dependencies.region: CC licence landscape is more developed in EU and UK following OER movement growth.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users integrate content types confidently.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): quality synthesis requires quality evaluation of source material
dc-3-3 (Copyright and licences): adaptation rights and attribution are integral
assessability: Literature reviews, adapted teaching resources, data integration projects. Supervisors and module tutors assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users use AI tools (Elicit, ChatGPT, Copilot) to assist with synthesis: AI-generated outlines reviewed and substantiated with original analysis, AI summarisation followed by critical cross-checking against primary sources, with explicit documentation of where AI contributed to the integration process.

observable_behaviours: Produces systematic literature reviews, meta-analyses, or evidence syntheses that integrate and critically re-present a large body of primary research with methodological rigour
Develops novel knowledge products by critically transforming, extending, or reconceptualising existing frameworks, datasets, or content bodies to create new scholarly or educational contributions
Leads teams or institutional projects in producing complex integrated content: curriculum frameworks, research data syntheses, or cross-institutional knowledge repositories
evidence_types: Systematic review, meta-analysis, or evidence synthesis report in peer-reviewed or institutional context
Curriculum framework, research synthesis, or knowledge repository produced through leadership of a complex integration project

common_misconceptions.misconception: A systematic review is a comprehensive summary of existing research
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: A systematic review is a methodologically rigorous primary research output with its own search strategy, inclusion criteria, quality appraisal, and synthesis methodology; it is not a summary but an original piece of research

common_misconceptions.misconception: Re-elaborating existing content is intellectually inferior to producing wholly original content
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Evidence synthesis, curriculum design based on existing knowledge, and adaptive re-use of frameworks are high-value intellectual contributions that advance knowledge as significantly as novel empirical research

context_dependencies.role: Research-active staff leading evidence synthesis. Curriculum designers and learning technologists producing complex educational content. Research data specialists creating data integration outputs.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Systematic review methodology is most formalised in health sciences. All disciplines engage with evidence synthesis at advanced level in different forms.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Doctoral and postdoctoral level in HE.
context_dependencies.region: PROSPERO systematic review registration and Cochrane methodology are UK/EU-led but globally adopted.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence; differentiator is methodological rigour and scholarly contribution.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): systematic search is prerequisite for systematic synthesis
dc-1-2 (Evaluating information): systematic appraisal of source quality is integral to evidence synthesis
assessability: Peer review of synthesis outputs, systematic review protocols, curriculum validation. Research supervisors and methodologists assess.
ai_integration_note: Advanced re-elaborators critically integrate AI-assisted synthesis tools (Elicit, Research Rabbit) into their methodological pipeline with explicit documentation of their role, while contributing to emerging methodological guidance on the appropriate use of AI in evidence synthesis.

observable_behaviours: Shapes the methodology and practice of knowledge synthesis in their field through landmark publications, new frameworks, or contributions to evidence synthesis standards and consortia
Leads transformative institutional knowledge integration projects that reconceptualise how research evidence and educational content are produced, curated, and shared
Contributes to scholarly discourse on the epistemology of evidence synthesis and AI-mediated knowledge integration
evidence_types: Methodological paper on knowledge synthesis or evidence integration, widely cited or adopted in the field
Leadership of a national or international evidence synthesis consortium or knowledge integration initiative

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced synthesis competence is the exclusive domain of information scientists
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Domain expertise combined with methodological sophistication defines highly advanced synthesis; content expertise is irreplaceable in determining what is worth synthesising and how to interpret results

common_misconceptions.misconception: AI will make human synthesis expertise redundant
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: AI can automate screening and data extraction tasks but cannot replace the conceptual framing, interpretive judgement, and domain expertise that define excellent evidence synthesis; highly advanced practitioners direct and critically evaluate AI contributions

context_dependencies.role: Senior researchers, methodology leaders, evidence synthesis infrastructure leads.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Health sciences, education, social policy, environmental science for evidence synthesis leadership.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE.
context_dependencies.region: Global evidence synthesis community (Cochrane, Campbell, EPPI-Centre).
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 1 competencies
All Area 3 competencies
assessability: Publication record, methodological contributions, consortium leadership.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the discourse on what AI-assisted knowledge synthesis means for scholarly epistemology: how knowledge claims produced through AI-mediated integration differ from those produced through traditional review methods, and what standards of transparency, reproducibility, and critical evaluation are required.

observable_behaviours: Understands that most online content is protected by copyright and cannot be freely reproduced, even for academic purposes, without permission or appropriate licence
Attributes sources and images used in academic work, using reference lists and captions, even when the legal requirement to do so is not fully understood
Avoids downloading and sharing copyrighted media (films, music, textbooks) through unauthorised channels
evidence_types: Academic submission with reference list showing basic attribution practice
Digital content produced for a module that uses only images and media the student knows they have permission to use

common_misconceptions.misconception: Anything freely available online is free to use
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Freely accessible content is not the same as openly licensed content; most content online is copyright-protected even when it can be viewed without payment

common_misconceptions.misconception: Academic use (educational purposes) means you can use any content freely
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Fair dealing and fair use are limited exceptions with specific conditions; they do not provide blanket permission for educational use of any copyrighted material

context_dependencies.role: Students learning about academic attribution. Educators using materials in teaching must comply with CLA licence. Professional services staff using third-party content in communications.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation at basic level though consequences differ: a music student using unlicensed audio in a project has different implications than a student using an unattributed quote.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE. Academic integrity induction covers copyright basics.
context_dependencies.region: UK copyright law (CDPA 1988) and EU Copyright Directive differ in significant ways; US fair use is more permissive than UK fair dealing. International students face navigating multiple systems.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may not encounter this issue; moderate-confidence users who create more digital content face it more acutely.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-1 (Developing digital content): content creation always involves copyright considerations
dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies): sharing content involves copyright compliance
assessability: Attribution practice in submitted work. Academic integrity modules include assessment of copyright understanding.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users typically do not consider the copyright implications of AI-generated content: who owns AI-generated text or images, whether training data copyright concerns are relevant, or what the rights status of AI outputs is under their institutional or national law.

observable_behaviours: Applies Creative Commons licence types correctly when sharing their own work, selecting the appropriate licence (CC BY, CC BY-NC, CC BY-SA) based on their sharing intentions
Identifies and applies the conditions of different licences when reusing others' content: understanding what CC BY requires vs CC BY-ND vs All Rights Reserved
Navigates institutional licence agreements (CLA educational licence, JISC content deals) to understand what content can be used in teaching and how
evidence_types: Work published or shared with a CC licence correctly applied
Teaching resource or research output demonstrating compliant use of licensed content with correct attribution

common_misconceptions.misconception: Creative Commons licences transfer copyright to the public
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: CC licences are permission frameworks that allow specific reuse while the creator retains copyright; the creator can still change the licence or use the work commercially; CC is not the same as public domain

common_misconceptions.misconception: If you find an image in Google Images, the licence displayed there is definitive
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Google Images licence filter is helpful but not authoritative; licence information must be verified at the source; many images are incorrectly tagged in search indexes

context_dependencies.role: Educators creating and sharing OERs. Researchers publishing open access with CC licences. Students sharing creative or research work online.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Creative arts and media face more complex copyright landscapes (moral rights, performance rights, synchronisation rights). STEM deals mainly with publication copyright and data licensing.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and all staff who create or share content.
context_dependencies.region: UK and EU have different copyright exceptions. The US TEACH Act differs from UK fair dealing. Compliance depends heavily on jurisdiction.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users can navigate licence databases; high-confidence users research edge cases independently.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-2 (Sharing): open sharing requires correct licence application
dc-3-2 (Integrating and re-elaborating): adapting content requires licence compliance
assessability: Licence choices in shared content, open access publication practice. Research development teams and copyright advisors assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users begin to grapple with the copyright ambiguity of AI-generated content: whether AI-generated text is copyrightable, how to apply a licence to content that may incorporate others' work through training data, and whether their institution's IP policies cover AI-assisted outputs.

observable_behaviours: Advises colleagues and students on copyright compliance, licence selection, and IP ownership in complex content creation scenarios (co-authored works, AI-assisted content, student-generated content)
Navigates publisher agreements, institutional copyright transfer agreements, and open access policies to maximise author rights while meeting funder and institutional obligations
Designs institutional processes or guidelines for copyright compliance in content creation, teaching, and research sharing contexts
evidence_types: Copyright guidance document, workshop, or policy contribution developed for institutional audience
Evidence of successfully negotiating or advising on complex copyright situations (publisher agreements, AI-generated content IP, student IP)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Copyright advice is always straightforward and there is a single correct answer
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Copyright law is jurisdiction-specific, contested, and evolving rapidly, particularly regarding AI; expert practitioners acknowledge uncertainty and advise on risk management, not just compliance

common_misconceptions.misconception: Using an AI tool that was trained on copyrighted material makes any output automatically infringing
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: The copyright status of AI training data use and AI outputs is unsettled law in most jurisdictions; the answer depends on jurisdiction, use case, and the specific AI system; oversimplification in either direction is inaccurate

context_dependencies.role: Copyright advisors, research development staff, librarians, academic staff with IP expertise.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Law and information science as disciplinary homes; applicable across all disciplines where content is created and shared.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Institutional specialists and senior academic staff.
context_dependencies.region: UK IPO guidance, EU Copyright Directive, and US copyright law must all be understood for international collaborations.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence; differentiator is legal and policy knowledge.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies): advanced sharing requires advanced copyright management
dc-3-2 (Integrating and re-elaborating): complex synthesis projects require sophisticated licence navigation
assessability: Policy documents, advisory records, professional recognition. Copyright specialists assess.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners develop institutional guidance on the copyright implications of AI in content creation, addressing training data rights, output ownership, moral rights, and the evolving legal landscape for generative AI in academic and creative contexts.

observable_behaviours: Contributes to the development of copyright law, open licensing frameworks, or IP policy at national or international level through publications, advocacy, or formal advisory roles
Shapes the scholarly or policy discourse on AI and copyright: training data rights, AI output ownership, and the implications for HE content creation and research
Leads institutional or sector-wide intellectual property strategy, addressing AI-generated works, student IP rights, and open knowledge infrastructure
evidence_types: Published scholarly or policy work on copyright law, open licensing, or AI and IP
Formal advisory role with a rights body, government body, or international standards organisation

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced copyright competence means knowing all copyright law
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: At this level, competence involves shaping policy and law, not just knowing it; the contribution is to the evolution of the framework, not compliance with a fixed one

common_misconceptions.misconception: Open licensing is primarily a technical matter
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Open licensing is a political and economic matter as much as a technical one; it concerns power relations between creators, platforms, and users; highly advanced practitioners engage with these dimensions

context_dependencies.role: IP specialists, technology lawyers, open access advocates, senior librarians.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Law, information science, digital humanities.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Specialist and research-intensive HE.
context_dependencies.region: EU Copyright Directive, UK IPO, WIPO international frameworks.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 3 competencies
dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies)
assessability: Policy contributions, published work, formal roles.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the legal and policy framework for AI and copyright, contributing to the most consequential questions about what AI training data use means for creative rights, how AI-generated works should be classified, and what institutional and national IP policies must do to remain fit for purpose in an age of generative AI.

observable_behaviours: Understands that software and digital systems follow logical instructions and that computational processes can be decomposed into steps
Creates simple automated sequences using no-code tools (VLE quiz logic, mail merge, conditional formatting in Excel, automated reminders in calendar apps)
Follows a written algorithm or set of instructions to complete a digital task, recognising when the instructions are not producing the expected outcome
evidence_types: VLE quiz with branching logic or conditional release rules configured by the user
Excel spreadsheet using IF statements or conditional formatting to automate a basic task

common_misconceptions.misconception: Computational thinking is only relevant to computer scientists
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Computational thinking (decomposition, pattern recognition, abstraction, algorithm design) is applicable to problem-solving in every discipline; HE students and staff benefit from these skills in data analysis, process design, and systematic thinking

common_misconceptions.misconception: Programming is the same as computational thinking
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Computational thinking is a problem-solving approach; programming is one tool for implementing it; you can think computationally without writing code, and you can write code without thinking computationally

context_dependencies.role: Educators configure VLE logic and automated communications. Students complete basic data analysis tasks in Excel or SPSS. Professional services staff use mail merge, workflow automation, and spreadsheet automation.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM students encounter computational thinking in quantitative methods. Social sciences use it in data analysis. Humanities use it in digital humanities projects.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Basic level is achievable by all HE students and staff; the entry point varies by discipline.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users avoid anything that looks like programming; moderate-confidence users use no-code automation tools independently.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-5-1 (Identifying and solving technical problems): basic computational thinking supports basic troubleshooting
dc-5-2 (Identifying digital technology needs): understanding what computers can do informs technology selection
assessability: Practical tasks: automated spreadsheet configuration, VLE quiz logic, no-code workflow setup. Module tutors and IT skills instructors assess.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may use AI-generated code snippets (ChatGPT, Copilot) without understanding what the code does, treating AI-generated scripts as black boxes; this creates risk when the code produces unexpected results and the user cannot diagnose or correct it.

observable_behaviours: Writes and adapts simple scripts or programmes in a scripting language (Python, R, MATLAB, SQL) to automate data processing, analysis, or reporting tasks relevant to their academic role
Applies computational thinking to break down a complex research or professional task into discrete, automatable steps, identifying where computation adds value and where human judgement is required
Uses version control (Git) or equivalent tools to manage code development, enabling collaboration and reproducibility of computational work
evidence_types: Python or R script used for data cleaning, analysis, or visualisation in a research or coursework context
GitHub repository showing version-controlled code for a research or coursework project

common_misconceptions.misconception: Intermediate programming means writing code from scratch without help
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Effective programmers at any level use documentation, Stack Overflow, and increasingly AI code assistants; competence is about understanding, adapting, and evaluating code, not unaided recall of syntax

common_misconceptions.misconception: If a script produces a result, the result is correct
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Scripts can produce plausible but incorrect results due to logic errors, data quality issues, or inappropriate statistical choices; checking outputs against expected results and understanding the method behind the script is essential

context_dependencies.role: Researchers use Python, R, or MATLAB for data analysis. Educators create computational teaching materials. Professional services staff write SQL queries or Power Automate workflows.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM subjects: Python, R, MATLAB are standard. Social sciences: R, Python, SPSS scripting. Humanities: Python for text analysis, corpus linguistics tools. Digital humanities increasingly require scripting skills.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate researchers and quantitative methods students.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation in core skills; tool preferences vary by discipline and institution.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users develop scripting skills with encouragement; high-confidence users extend independently.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-1 (Browsing, searching): database API access links searching and computational thinking
dc-1-3 (Managing information): version control is a form of information management for code
assessability: Code submissions, repository activity, practical programming tasks. Supervisors and module tutors assess through code review.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate programmers use AI coding assistants (GitHub Copilot, ChatGPT, Cursor) to generate code while developing the skill to read, understand, and critically evaluate AI-generated code before running it; they understand that AI coding assistants produce plausible but sometimes incorrect code.

observable_behaviours: Designs, builds, and documents complex computational workflows, data pipelines, or software tools used in research or educational contexts, ensuring reproducibility and code quality
Applies software engineering best practices to computational research: testing, documentation, modular design, dependency management, and open code publication
Teaches or advises on computational methods, code review, and reproducible research practices, mentoring less experienced colleagues or students in computational skills development
evidence_types: Published or shared codebase (GitHub repository) for a research project meeting open code standards with documentation, tests, and reproducibility instructions
Teaching or training materials for computational methods courses or workshops delivered to researchers or students

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced computational thinking means writing the most complex or efficient code
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Advanced competence emphasises readability, reproducibility, and correctness over performance optimisation; code that others can understand, maintain, and reproduce is more valuable in most research contexts than highly optimised but opaque code

common_misconceptions.misconception: Reproducibility is the developer's problem, not the researcher's
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Reproducibility is a core scientific norm; researchers who use computational methods bear responsibility for ensuring their computational pipeline can be reproduced; outsourcing this to a developer does not transfer the epistemological obligation

context_dependencies.role: Research software engineers, computational researchers, data scientists in HE, educators with computational pedagogy specialisms.
context_dependencies.subject_area: STEM and quantitative social sciences are primary contexts; digital humanities and computational linguistics are growing.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Doctoral, postdoctoral, and research software engineering roles.
context_dependencies.region: UK Software Sustainability Institute and EU Open Science requirements shape expectations for computational research outputs.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence is typical; differentiator is software engineering discipline and reproducibility commitment.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-2 (Integrating and re-elaborating): complex data synthesis requires computational methods
dc-1-3 (Managing information): research data management integrates with computational pipeline management
assessability: Code review, published computational research outputs, training delivery, peer recognition. RSE community assessment and journal code review standards.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners critically and productively integrate AI coding tools into their workflows, documenting AI tool use in code provenance, reviewing AI-generated code with the same rigour applied to any code, and contributing to emerging community norms for AI-assisted computational research.

observable_behaviours: Contributes to the development of research software, tools, or platforms used by a broad community of researchers, potentially as an open source contributor or research infrastructure builder
Shapes the discourse on computational reproducibility, research software engineering, or AI-assisted coding in HE through publications, policy contributions, or community leadership
Leads institutional or national initiatives on computational research infrastructure, research software engineering professionalisation, or AI-literacy in computational research
evidence_types: Widely used open source research software, cited computational tool, or major contribution to research computing infrastructure
Published work on computational research methodology, research software engineering, or AI-assisted coding in research contexts

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced computational competence means being a software engineer or computer scientist
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Domain researchers who are highly computationally competent contribute their disciplinary expertise to the design of computational methods; the combination of domain and computational expertise is the distinctive competence, not technical skill alone

common_misconceptions.misconception: AI coding assistants will eventually make programming expertise unnecessary
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: AI coding tools shift the nature of programming expertise rather than eliminating it; understanding code, making sound design decisions, and evaluating AI-generated outputs requires deep computational knowledge that AI tools cannot substitute for themselves

context_dependencies.role: Research software engineers, computational method leaders, data science leads, digital research infrastructure specialists.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Bioinformatics, computational social science, digital humanities, astrophysics, climate science among the most computationally advanced.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE and national research facilities.
context_dependencies.region: EOSC (European Open Science Cloud), UK Research Infrastructure, and national supercomputing facilities are the primary policy contexts.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 3 competencies
All Area 5 competencies
assessability: Research impact, software citation, community recognition, publications.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals contribute to shaping the future of AI-augmented computational research: what it means for reproducibility when AI-generated code is integrated into scientific workflows, how the research software engineering community should respond to AI coding assistants, and what new methodological standards are needed.

observable_behaviours: Keeps operating system and software on personal devices updated when prompted, understanding that updates often contain security patches
Uses a password or PIN to lock personal devices and does not share device access credentials with others
Avoids installing software from unknown or unverified sources and can identify obviously suspicious installation prompts
evidence_types: Device security settings showing password lock and automatic updates enabled
Completion of institutional device security awareness training

common_misconceptions.misconception: Antivirus software alone is sufficient to protect a device
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Antivirus addresses one threat vector; device security requires layered protection including software updates, access control, network hygiene, and phishing awareness

common_misconceptions.misconception: University-owned devices are the IT department's responsibility and personal security habits do not matter
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Device security on institutionally connected personal devices requires active user participation; IT departments cannot protect against user-enabled threats like phishing clicks or weak passwords without user cooperation

context_dependencies.role: All HE users. Students using personal devices for institutional access. Educators managing course delivery devices. Professional services staff handling institutional data on personal or institutional devices.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation at basic level.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE. Institutional onboarding covers this.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation in basic hygiene; institutional policy varies.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may not update devices, assuming it causes problems. Moderate-confidence users follow prompts.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): device security is a prerequisite for data protection on those devices
assessability: IT audit data (device compliance), security training completion records. IT services and security teams assess at scale.
ai_integration_note: At this level, AI-specific threats (AI-generated phishing emails, AI-powered malware) are beyond the user's awareness; basic device protection focuses on traditional threat vectors.

observable_behaviours: Configures multi-factor authentication (MFA) on institutional and personal accounts, understanding why single-password authentication is insufficient
Identifies and reports phishing attempts and social engineering attacks to the appropriate institutional team, including AI-generated phishing messages that mimic legitimate communications
Uses institutional VPN appropriately when accessing university resources on public or unsecured networks, understanding why network hygiene matters for device and data security
evidence_types: MFA enabled on all institutional accounts, evidenced through IT system records
Reported phishing attempt with appropriate institutional follow-up

common_misconceptions.misconception: MFA is an inconvenience that only matters for high-security contexts
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: MFA is now a standard security baseline for all accounts; the overhead is minimal and the protection against credential theft is substantial across all account types

common_misconceptions.misconception: If a phishing email looks professional and contains accurate personal details, it must be legitimate
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: AI-generated phishing emails can be indistinguishable from legitimate communications and may include personal details sourced from data breaches; professional appearance is no longer a reliable trust indicator

context_dependencies.role: All HE staff and students. Researchers with access to sensitive data face higher-stakes device security requirements.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Health sciences and clinical research have additional device security obligations where patient data may be processed.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for all HE students and staff from induction.
context_dependencies.region: NCSC (UK) and ENISA (EU) guidance shapes intermediate device security expectations. GDPR creates legal obligations for data breach prevention.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users manage MFA and VPN independently. High-confidence users extend to network analysis.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): device security failures are a major cause of data breaches
assessability: IT compliance monitoring, security incident records, phishing simulation exercise results. IT security teams assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users are aware that AI tools are used to generate convincing phishing content and that AI-powered attack tools have lowered the sophistication threshold for social engineering attacks; they apply heightened scepticism to digital communications that request action or credentials.

observable_behaviours: Conducts or supports device security risk assessments for research projects or departmental contexts, identifying vulnerabilities and recommending mitigations proportionate to the data sensitivity and threat landscape
Designs and delivers device security awareness training for colleagues or students, tailored to the specific threat environment and risk profile of the HE context
Advises on device security implications of new technology adoption (AI tools, cloud services, IoT research equipment) for institutional or research environments
evidence_types: Device security risk assessment or policy contribution for a research project or departmental context
Security awareness training materials developed and delivered to a staff or student audience

common_misconceptions.misconception: Device security is entirely an IT department responsibility in institutional contexts
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: While IT departments manage institutional infrastructure, individual users and research teams bear significant security responsibility for their devices, research data, and access practices; security culture is a shared organisational responsibility

common_misconceptions.misconception: Security measures always trade off against usability and should be minimised for productivity
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Well-designed security measures reduce overall risk without commensurate productivity costs; security-as-afterthought is more costly in the long run than security-by-design

context_dependencies.role: IT security staff, research data officers, information governance specialists, academics with research security obligations.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Research involving sensitive data (health records, personal data, national security-relevant research) faces the most demanding device security requirements.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Mid-career and senior HE staff; IT specialists.
context_dependencies.region: UK DSIT research security requirements, NCSC guidance, and EU NIS2 Directive create specific institutional obligations.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence; differentiator is security expertise and risk assessment capability.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy): advanced device security and data protection are inseparable at institutional level
dc-5-1 (Identifying and solving technical problems): advanced troubleshooting includes security incident response
assessability: Risk assessments, training delivery, policy contributions, incident response records.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners assess the device security implications of AI tool adoption: what data AI tools collect from devices, how AI-generated attack content has changed the threat landscape, and how institutional AI usage policies must address device and endpoint security.

observable_behaviours: Shapes institutional, sector, or national device security strategy and policy for HE, contributing to standards, frameworks, and governance at scale
Publishes or presents on the evolving device security landscape in HE, including AI-enabled threats, research security, and the intersection of institutional and personal device security
Leads major institutional security transformation initiatives or contributes to sector-wide security resilience programmes
evidence_types: Institutional security strategy or policy document with evidence of authorship
Published work on HE security or contribution to sector security standards

common_misconceptions.misconception: Device security expertise is purely technical and separated from institutional governance
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: At this level, security is fundamentally a governance, culture, and risk management challenge; technical expertise serves strategic and organisational decisions

common_misconceptions.misconception: HE institutions face the same device security challenges as corporate organisations
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: HE's open culture, large mobile student population, research data obligations, and mixed institutional/personal device environment creates a distinct and particularly complex security landscape

context_dependencies.role: CISOs, IT directors, national sector security leads.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Cross-institutional.
context_dependencies.institution_level: All types but leadership roles in research-intensive institutions.
context_dependencies.region: UK NCSC, JISC security services, EU NIS2 are primary policy contexts.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-2 (Protecting personal data and privacy)
All Area 4 competencies
assessability: Strategic leadership roles, publications, sector contributions.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape national and sectoral responses to AI-enabled security threats: how HE institutions should respond to AI-powered social engineering, AI-generated deepfakes used for fraud, and the security implications of integrating AI systems into research and administrative infrastructure.

observable_behaviours: Understands that personal data (name, email address, student ID) is a category requiring protection and does not share their own or others' personal data unnecessarily
Reviews and manages basic privacy settings on social media platforms, restricting profile visibility to appropriate audiences
Reads and follows institutional data protection guidance when handling information about other students or staff in academic work
evidence_types: Privacy settings review activity completed as part of digital skills induction
Academic work avoiding unnecessary disclosure of identifiable information about other individuals

common_misconceptions.misconception: Only sensitive categories of data (health information, financial data) need protection
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Under GDPR and equivalent frameworks, all personal data (any information that identifies a living individual) requires protection; the type of protection varies by sensitivity, but all personal data has legal obligations

common_misconceptions.misconception: If you give consent for data use once, the organisation can keep using it indefinitely for any purpose
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Data protection law requires purpose limitation and the right to withdraw consent; organisations must specify what they will use data for and for how long

context_dependencies.role: All HE users. Students handling peer information in group projects. Educators handling student data.
