context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation at basic level.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE; covered in student induction.
context_dependencies.region: GDPR (EU/UK) creates specific rights. US FERPA protects student records differently. International students at UK/EU institutions are protected by GDPR regardless of nationality.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may be unaware of privacy settings. Moderate-confidence users manage them when reminded.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-2-6 (Managing digital identity): personal data management and identity management are intertwined
dc-4-1 (Protecting devices): device security is a prerequisite for data protection
assessability: Privacy settings review, data protection training completion, academic work quality. Compliance training records.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users typically do not consider what personal data they share with AI tools: entering names, email addresses, or student details into AI chat tools may involve data transfer to third-party servers without institutional data protection oversight.

observable_behaviours: Applies GDPR principles (lawful basis, purpose limitation, data minimisation, storage limitation) to their own practice when collecting or handling personal data in research or professional activities
Anonymises or pseudonymises research data appropriately before sharing, using standard techniques and understanding the limitations of anonymisation
Completes and files a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) for research projects involving personal data, with guidance from institutional Data Protection Officers
evidence_types: DPIA document completed for a research project with personal data
Anonymised research dataset shared under appropriate licence with documented anonymisation process

common_misconceptions.misconception: Anonymisation removes all privacy risk from data
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Anonymisation reduces re-identification risk but does not eliminate it, particularly in small populations or when data can be combined with other sources (the mosaic effect); absolute anonymisation is often technically impossible

common_misconceptions.misconception: Consent is always required for research involving personal data
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Research can use other lawful bases (public task, legitimate interests) under GDPR; consent is one option but not always the most appropriate or feasible basis for research data processing

context_dependencies.role: Researchers collecting human participant data. Professional services staff handling student records, HR data, or financial information. Educators designing assessments that involve personal data.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Health sciences face the most stringent data protection requirements. Social sciences handle sensitive personal data frequently. Law and business students engage with GDPR as academic content.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate researchers and professional services staff with data access.
context_dependencies.region: GDPR is the dominant framework in EU and UK. UK GDPR post-Brexit maintains equivalent protections. US HIPAA applies in health contexts. Region-specific knowledge is HIGH impact for this competency.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users follow institutional guidance. High-confidence users apply principles independently.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-1-3 (Managing information): data management plans integrate data protection obligations
dc-2-2 (Sharing through digital technologies): data sharing requires privacy compliance
assessability: DPIA submissions, research ethics applications, data sharing agreements. Research ethics committees and DPOs assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate users apply data protection principles to AI tool use: checking whether institutional AI tools are GDPR-compliant before entering personal data, understanding data residency and third-party processing implications, and contributing to institutional AI data governance discussions.

observable_behaviours: Designs and implements data protection frameworks for research projects, institutional systems, or service design, applying privacy-by-design principles and proportionate risk management
Advises colleagues, students, or junior researchers on GDPR compliance, lawful basis selection, and privacy risk management for complex data scenarios
Contributes to institutional data governance: drafting data protection policies, contributing to institutional RPA (Record of Processing Activities), supporting DPO activities
evidence_types: Data protection policy or framework document contributed to institutional governance
Advisory record showing expert guidance provided on complex data protection scenarios (AI tools, international data transfers, sensitive data processing)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced data protection expertise means knowing all privacy law in detail
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Data protection expertise at this level is about applying principles to novel situations, managing risk, and designing systems that protect privacy by default; legal detail supports but does not define this expertise

common_misconceptions.misconception: Privacy-by-design is a compliance burden that slows down research and innovation
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Privacy-by-design prevents costly remediation later and builds trust with research participants, users, and regulators; integrating privacy into system design from the start is almost always cheaper and more effective than retrofitting it

context_dependencies.role: Data Protection Officers, Research Data Managers, Information Governance Managers, research ethics leads.
context_dependencies.subject_area: All disciplines with human participant research; health sciences and social sciences most intensively.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Specialist roles in HE.
context_dependencies.region: GDPR is the dominant framework; specialist knowledge of UK adequacy decisions, SCCs (Standard Contractual Clauses) for international transfers, and AI Act privacy provisions is expected.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence; differentiator is legal and governance expertise.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-4-1 (Protecting devices): data protection requires secure device environments
dc-2-6 (Managing digital identity): identity governance and data protection intersect
assessability: Policy documents, DPIA quality, advisory records, DPO review.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners design institutional frameworks for AI and data protection: assessing whether AI tools meet GDPR requirements, managing Article 22 implications of automated decision-making, and contributing to institutional AI governance that integrates data protection obligations with AI transparency and accountability requirements.

observable_behaviours: Shapes national or international data protection policy, contributing to ICO guidance, EU data protection authority decisions, or academic scholarship on privacy law and governance
Leads institutional data protection transformation, embedding privacy-by-design as a cultural norm rather than a compliance exercise
Contributes to scholarly or policy discourse on emerging data protection challenges: AI-generated synthetic data, biometric data in HE, algorithmic profiling of students
evidence_types: Published scholarship on privacy law, data governance, or AI and data protection
Contribution to national or international data protection guidance or regulatory framework

common_misconceptions.misconception: Data protection at the highest level is purely a legal matter for specialists

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced technology identification means always being an early adopter
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Strategic restraint in technology adoption is as important as strategic adoption; highly advanced practitioners recognise when emerging technology should not be adopted and can articulate why with evidence

common_misconceptions.misconception: Technology needs identification is a technical or IT function
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: At the highest level, needs identification integrates academic, pedagogical, ethical, and institutional considerations; it is a leadership function, not a technical one

context_dependencies.role: CIOs, VCs and DVC with digital portfolios, technology ethics scholars, digital strategy consultants.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Cross-institutional.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive and policy-leading HE.
context_dependencies.region: EU AI Act, UK AI Strategy, JISC digital strategy guidance.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 5 competencies
All Area 4 competencies
assessability: Publications, policy contributions, institutional leadership.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the national and international frameworks for responsible AI adoption in HE: what evaluation standards, governance structures, and regulatory requirements should govern AI tool adoption, and how the field can develop shared approaches to AI needs identification that serve academic, ethical, and sustainability goals.

competency_name: Identifying creative solutions using digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Experiments with unfamiliar digital tools or features to find new ways of completing academic or professional tasks, rather than defaulting to familiar approaches when they are insufficient
Generates at least one digital alternative to a manual or analogue solution when prompted to consider digital options
Combines two or more existing digital tools in a basic way to achieve a task that neither tool could accomplish alone (e.g. using Padlet for brainstorming and then copying outputs to a Word document)
evidence_types: Assignment or project documentation showing a novel (for the student) use of digital tools to address a specific challenge
Reflection on a digital problem-solving experience where an experimental approach was tried

common_misconceptions.misconception: Creative digital solutions require advanced technical knowledge
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Creative problem solving at a basic level involves curiosity, experimentation, and willingness to combine familiar tools in new ways; advanced technical skill enhances but does not prerequisite creative digital thinking

common_misconceptions.misconception: There is usually one correct digital solution to any given problem
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Multiple digital approaches can solve any given problem; creative solution identification involves generating and comparing options rather than seeking a single correct answer

context_dependencies.role: Students experimenting with digital tools for assignments. Educators trying new teaching approaches. Professional services staff finding digital efficiencies.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Creative and design disciplines develop this disposition earlier. STEM students apply it to quantitative problem solving.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High-confidence users experiment more readily. Low-confidence users need scaffolded encouragement to experiment.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-5-2 (Identifying needs): creative solutions start from well-identified needs
dc-3-4 (Computational thinking): creative problem-solving and computational thinking are closely related
assessability: Project documentation, reflective essays, portfolio submissions. Tutors observe through assignment quality.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users may use AI tools creatively for problem-solving (using ChatGPT to brainstorm, DALL-E for visual ideation) but without systematic evaluation of whether the AI-assisted approach is the most appropriate or effective solution.

competency_name: Identifying creative solutions using digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Designs a novel digital workflow, tool combination, or process to address a specific academic or professional challenge, documenting the approach and its outcomes
Applies design thinking or structured creativity methods to identify digital solutions to HE challenges, including iterative prototyping and user testing of digital approaches
Critically evaluates the creative digital solutions of others (peer students' project approaches, published technology cases) and adapts relevant elements for their own contexts
evidence_types: Digital solution prototype or workflow design with documentation showing iterative development and user testing
Case study or reflective report on adapting a creative digital approach from one context to another

common_misconceptions.misconception: Creative solutions using AI automatically involve less human creativity
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Creative use of AI requires vision, curation, critical evaluation, and iteration; AI is a creative input, not a creative substitute; the quality of human-AI creative partnership depends on the quality of human direction

common_misconceptions.misconception: Intermediate creative problem solving means inventing genuinely new technologies
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Most valuable creative digital problem solving at this level involves novel application of existing technologies to new contexts; the creativity is in the application, not the invention

context_dependencies.role: Students designing digital projects and capstone work. Educators designing creative assessments and learning experiences. Researchers designing digital research methodologies.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Arts and design, education technology, digital humanities, and innovation-oriented business programmes most intensively.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and all academic staff.
context_dependencies.region: EU Digital Europe programme and UK digital innovation ecosystems create opportunities and frameworks for creative digital solution development.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High-confidence users explore more ambitiously. Structured creativity methods help moderate-confidence users engage systematically.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-1 (Developing digital content): creative digital solutions often involve creating new digital content or tools
dc-5-4 (Addressing digital competence needs): identifying competence gaps in others enables creative solution design
assessability: Project portfolios, design documentation, peer assessment. Educators and innovation coaches assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate practitioners design creative AI-human workflows: developing prompting strategies, tool combinations (AI generation + human curation + editing), and creative processes that leverage AI capabilities while maintaining human creative direction and quality control.

competency_name: Identifying creative solutions using digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Leads digital innovation projects that develop novel technological solutions to significant HE challenges: new assessment approaches, research methodology innovations, or service design breakthroughs
Designs and facilitates creative digital problem-solving processes for teams or cohorts, using structured innovation methodologies (hackathons, design sprints, co-design) in digital contexts
Critically contributes to institutional digital innovation strategy, evaluating where and how creative digital approaches can add the most value and what conditions enable successful innovation
evidence_types: Digital innovation project documentation showing development from problem identification through solution design, prototype, and evaluation
Facilitation record or report from a creative digital problem-solving initiative (hackathon, design sprint, co-design process)

common_misconceptions.misconception: Innovation always requires new technology
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Many significant HE innovations involve applying existing technology in new ways or to underserved contexts; the creative insight is in the application, not the technology

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced creative digital problem solving requires exceptional technical skill
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Advanced creative problem solving requires strategic thinking, facilitation skill, and domain expertise; technical capability is a resource to draw on, not the defining competence

context_dependencies.role: Innovation leads, learning technologists with innovation remit, research methodology specialists, academic entrepreneurs.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Design, education technology, digital humanities, social innovation.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Mid-career and senior HE staff.
context_dependencies.region: EU digital innovation ecosystems (EIC, Digital Innovation Hubs) and UK UKRI digital innovation funding shape the context.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence with breadth across tool types.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-3-4 (Computational thinking): advanced creative problem solving often involves designed computational workflows
dc-5-2 (Identifying technology needs): creative innovation starts from excellent needs identification
assessability: Innovation project outcomes, facilitation records, institutional impact.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners lead institutional AI innovation initiatives: identifying where AI creates genuinely novel capabilities for education and research, designing creative human-AI workflows, and contributing to the responsible innovation discourse around AI in HE.

competency_name: Identifying creative solutions using digital technologies
observable_behaviours: Shapes the field of digital innovation in HE through landmark projects, publications, or contributions to national and international innovation frameworks and funding landscapes
Contributes scholarly understanding of how creative digital problem solving and innovation occur in educational and research contexts, advancing theory and practice

Leads sector-wide transformation in how HE approaches digital innovation: embedding creative digital problem solving as an institutional capability and developing the next generation of digital innovators
evidence_types: Published research on digital innovation in HE or widely-adopted innovation framework
Leadership of a sector-transforming digital innovation initiative or programme

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced digital creativity means producing the most technologically sophisticated solutions
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: At this level, the contribution is conceptual and strategic: shaping how innovation is understood, supported, and institutionalised; the most impactful innovations are often conceptually simple and technically accessible

common_misconceptions.misconception: Generative AI will replace human creative problem solving
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Creative problem solving involves problem identification, value judgements, ethical navigation, and solution contextualisation that AI cannot perform independently; AI augments human creativity but does not replace the essentially human act of defining what problem is worth solving

context_dependencies.role: Innovation VPs, digital transformation leaders, research-active educational technologists.

context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive HE and innovation-leading institutions.

cross_competency_dependencies: All Area 5 competencies
All Area 3 competencies
assessability: Publications, sector leadership, innovation impact.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals contribute to defining what human creativity means in an age of generative AI, and how educational institutions should develop the creative capabilities that complement rather than compete with AI, shaping the future of human-AI creative collaboration in research and education.

competency_name: Identifying and addressing digital competence needs
observable_behaviours: Identifies gaps in their own digital skills when completing academic or professional tasks and seeks appropriate help or learning resources (tutorials, IT training, library workshops)
Completes digital skills training offered by the institution when it is relevant to their academic or professional needs
Reflects on a digital task that was difficult and identifies what they would need to learn to complete it more effectively in the future
evidence_types: Completion of institutional digital skills training or workshop
Personal development plan entry identifying a digital competence gap and a plan to address it

common_misconceptions.misconception: If you cannot figure out a digital tool quickly, you are not a digital person
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital competence is a learnable set of skills that develops over time with practice and support; the ability to recognise and address competence gaps is itself a form of digital sophistication

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital skills training is only necessary for people who are not naturally good with technology
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: All digital users have competence gaps; in a rapidly changing technological landscape, continuous digital skill development is necessary for everyone, regardless of their baseline confidence

context_dependencies.role: Students recognising academic digital skill needs. Educators recognising teaching technology gaps. Professional services staff recognising system proficiency needs.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation; self-aware learning is a universal HE competence.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Entry level for HE.
context_dependencies.region: Low variation.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Low-confidence users may be embarrassed to acknowledge digital gaps. Moderate-confidence users actively seek training.

cross_competency_dependencies: All other competencies: 5.4 is metacognitive and supports development across all other competencies
assessability: Training completion records, personal development plans, reflective essays. Personal tutors and academic skills staff assess.
ai_integration_note: At this level, users are beginning to identify AI literacy as a competence area requiring development: recognising that using AI tools effectively requires specific skills and seeking training in prompt design, AI output evaluation, and responsible AI use.

competency_name: Identifying and addressing digital competence needs
observable_behaviours: Conducts a structured self-assessment of their own digital competences using frameworks (DigComp, JISC BDC) and creates a targeted development plan
Identifies digital competence gaps in peers or team members and provides appropriate signposting or informal support (peer mentoring, resource sharing, co-learning)
Accesses and evaluates the quality of digital skills resources (MOOCs, institutional training, professional development offerings) and selects those most relevant to identified needs
evidence_types: Personal digital competence self-assessment and development plan using a recognised framework
Evidence of supporting a peer's digital competence development through mentoring, resource sharing, or co-learning

common_misconceptions.misconception: Self-assessment using a competence framework produces an objective measure of competence
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Self-assessment is subject to the Dunning-Kruger effect; unskilled individuals often overestimate their competence, while experts tend to underestimate; self-assessment is most useful when supplemented with observed evidence and peer feedback

common_misconceptions.misconception: Completing a digital skills course automatically resolves a competence gap
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Training provides knowledge and exposure; competence develops through applied practice in authentic contexts; course completion without application has limited lasting impact on capability

context_dependencies.role: Educators supporting student digital development. Researchers developing their own and team digital research skills. Professional services staff managing their own and team CPD.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Low variation in the metacognitive skill; subject-specific digital competence landscapes vary.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Expected for postgraduate students and all staff.
context_dependencies.region: DigComp (EU), JISC BDC (UK), and UNESCO CFT (global) are the primary competence frameworks referenced.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Moderate-confidence users engage with structured self-assessment. High-confidence users may resist frameworks that seem too basic.

cross_competency_dependencies: All other competencies: 5.4 provides the metacognitive layer for all other digital competence development
assessability: Self-assessment documents, development plans, peer support records. Supervisors and professional development teams assess.
ai_integration_note: Intermediate practitioners use AI literacy frameworks to structure their own and others' AI competence development: assessing AI-specific competence gaps (prompt design, AI output evaluation, AI ethics), seeking targeted AI literacy resources, and helping peers navigate the rapidly changing AI tool landscape.

competency_name: Identifying and addressing digital competence needs
observable_behaviours: Designs and delivers digital competence development programmes, workshops, or curricula for specific HE audiences, grounded in a theoretical understanding of digital literacy and competence frameworks
Conducts digital competence needs analysis for teams, departments, or student cohorts, using validated assessment approaches and translating findings into evidence-based development programmes
Evaluates the effectiveness of digital competence development interventions and uses evidence to iteratively improve provision
evidence_types: Digital competence development programme designed and delivered, with participant feedback and evaluation data
Needs analysis report for a team or student cohort with resulting development plan and implementation evidence

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital competence training should focus on tools rather than conceptual frameworks
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Tool-focused training requires constant updating as tools change; framework-grounded training develops transferable digital thinking that adapts to new tools; both are necessary but the conceptual foundation is more durable

common_misconceptions.misconception: Advanced digital skills trainers need to be the most technically skilled people in the room
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Advanced digital skills development is primarily about facilitating learning and growth; the facilitator role requires pedagogical skill and a growth mindset, not superiority across all digital competence domains

context_dependencies.role: Digital skills trainers, educational developers, academic skills advisors, research skills librarians.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Education, library and information science, organisational development.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Professional and specialist staff in HE.
context_dependencies.region: JISC digital capability service, DigComp education framework, and national digital skills strategies shape the training landscape.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: High confidence across multiple competence areas enables credibility and breadth in training.

cross_competency_dependencies: dc-5-2 (Identifying technology needs): understanding the tool landscape is necessary for effective needs assessment
All other Area 5 competencies: advanced 5.4 draws on all problem-solving competences
assessability: Training programme quality, participant feedback, evaluation reports, institutional recognition.
ai_integration_note: Advanced practitioners design AI literacy curricula and needs assessment frameworks for HE, addressing the rapidly evolving landscape of AI competences: what knowledge, skills, and attitudes are needed to use AI effectively and critically in research and educational contexts, and how these can be developed systematically.

competency_name: Identifying and addressing digital competence needs
observable_behaviours: Contributes to the development, validation, or revision of digital competence frameworks at national or international level (DigComp, JISC BDC, UNESCO CFT) through research, expert consultation, or policy advocacy
Publishes scholarly research on digital competence assessment, development, or the changing nature of digital literacy in AI-augmented environments
Shapes the strategic direction of digital capability development at institutional, sector, or national level, influencing policy, resource allocation, and professional norms
evidence_types: Published research on digital competence frameworks, assessment, or digital literacy theory and practice
Contribution to a national or international digital competence framework development or validation process

common_misconceptions.misconception: Digital competence frameworks, once established, provide a stable and sufficient basis for development
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: Digital competence frameworks require continuous review as technology evolves; frameworks that do not integrate AI literacy, data fluency, and emerging digital capabilities become rapidly outdated and mislead development priorities

common_misconceptions.misconception: Highly advanced digital competence support is only about training provision
common_misconceptions.why_wrong: At this level, the contribution is conceptual and political: defining what digital competence means, for whom, and in what contexts; training provision serves a larger strategic and pedagogical vision

context_dependencies.role: Digital literacy researchers, senior educational developers, framework authors, policy leads.
context_dependencies.subject_area: Education, information science, communication, technology studies.
context_dependencies.institution_level: Research-intensive and policy-leading HE.
context_dependencies.region: European Commission DigComp team, JRC, JISC, UNESCO, and national digital skills bodies.
context_dependencies.digital_confidence: Not a variable.

cross_competency_dependencies: All other competencies: 5.4 at the highest level is about shaping how digital competence itself is understood and developed
assessability: Publications, framework contributions, policy influence, sector leadership.
ai_integration_note: At this level, individuals shape the evolution of digital competence frameworks to address AI literacy: contributing to defining what it means to be digitally competent in an AI-saturated environment, and ensuring that frameworks like DigComp itself remain fit for purpose in a world where AI is transversally embedded in all digital competence areas.
